[[RunningHead]]

Integration in Psychotherapy: An Evolving Reality in Personality Disorder

Anthony Bateman

Anthony Bateman

Anthony Bateman  

Psychotherapy continues to be bedevilled by ideological schisms with practitioners apparently ignoring alternative conceptualizations and potentially superior interventions. However, I argue here that there is evidence of a rapprochement, both in theory and in practice, between cognitive therapy and psychoanalytic therapy, especially within the domain of personality disorder, which may lead to the development of integrative psychotherapy. Cognitive therapy has begun to encompass an interpersonal approach within its theoretical base. Similarly, psychoanalytic therapy increasingly uses an interpersonal formulation of the process of therapy. The therapeutic alliance is emphasized equally and process research suggests that interventions, when given by experienced practitioners, are not as dissimilar as ‘brand-named’ therapies imply. Continued refinement of process psychotherapy research could lead to true integration of efficacious therapeutic interventions. But translating research findings into practice will necessitate psychotherapists opening themselves up to each others' ideas.

The Seduction of Therapy

Rob Weatherill

Rob Weatherill

12 Crosthwaite Park East, Dun Laoghaire. [email: robweath@indigo.ie; website: http://indigo.ie/~robweath/homepage.html]

Rob Weatherill  

This paper claims that the psychotherapeutic situation is haunted by the erotic transference which arises from the artificial setting of the analysis itself, which, with its care, attention and listening, reinvokes the primal seduction (Laplanche) or transformation (Bollas) of the infant by the mother. Freud wanted to distance himself from seduction, coming to prefer instead the productive work of analysis in a state of deprivation. I argue that modern practitioners and trainings (ironically, seductive in themselves!), responding to consumer demand and fearful of litigation, attempt to remove all risk from the ‘professional’ setting of the therapy. Here, the great danger is the loss of the radical anarchic otherness of the unconscious, indeed the endless play of seduction itself, which alone animates the heart of the analytic process. Finally, psychosis is equated with the loss of seduction, as is our current cultural fascination with IT - cool seduction (Baudrillard).

Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT) is a form of brief psychotherapy, developed for the treatment of depression. Controlled outcome trials have demonstrated its efficacy in the treatment of acute depression in psychiatric outpatient settings, in primary care settings and with special populations such as depressed adolescents and depressed elderly patients. In the depressed elderly IPT has the advantage, compared to antidepressant medication, of producing fewer side-effects and fewer drop-outs from treatment. Continuation/ maintenance treatment with IPT (IPT-CM) appears to be effective in reducing relapse rates of patients with an established history of recurrent depression (Markowitz 1998).

A standardized manual for IPT for depression is widely available (Klerman et al. 1984). This was developed for use in controlled treatment trials, carried out by the National Institute of Mental Health in the USA. The initial two to three sessions (‘initial phase’) consist of an assessment which includes, first, a detailed review of depressive symptoms and, second, the ‘Interpersonal Inventory’, a detailed review of past and, particularly, all current relationships.

The Unconscious and Psychosis: Some Considerations on the Psychoanalytic Theory of Psychosis

Franco De Masi

The author contends that the various psychoanalytic theories and techniques employ different models of the unconscious, each relating to a different unconscious reality describable in terms of specific mental functions. He reviews, in particular, the Freudian dynamic unconscious, based on repression; the Kleinian unconscious, which adds the notions of unconscious fantasy and splitting of the object; B ion's conception of the unconscious as a mental function of which the subject is unaware but which can formulate thoughts and metabolize emotions; and the neuroscientific view of the unconscious as coinciding with that of which one is unaware and not with the Freudian repressed. The author thus distinguishes between the dynamic and the emotional unconscious and between ‘unconscious’ and ‘unaware’, and notes the role of distortion of the ‘unaware’ perceptions involved in the analytic relationship in the impasse situation. He is particularly concerned to show that, whereas neurosis involves the dynamic unconscious, psychosis alters the emotional unconscious, the entity underlying the sense of identity and the ‘unaware’ consciousness of existence. In psychosis the emotional unconscious is blinded so that the patient is conscious but lacks awareness. The dynamic unconscious is also affected. After presenting two case histories, the author draws attention to the need for further clinical and theoretical research in this field.



International Journal of Psycho-Analysis81, 37, 2000

Sexuality and Perversion a Hundred Years on: Discovering What Freud Discovered

Michael Parsons

The author considers how Freud's original formulation of the sexual drive may be understood in contemporary terms. Parallels between psychoanalysis, art history and the social and natural sciences underline the idea of sexuality as a construct that can be revisited. The nature of sexuality depends on how its irreducible biological basis is interpreted by a particular society at a particular time. The importance of revisiting is illustrated by Klein's concept of a position, which revisits the theoretical construct of a developmental stage. Freud's own construction of sexuality is based on his view of drive as comprising source, aim and object. Freud, in the Darwinian climate of his time, considered the object in terms of whether it served the fulfilment of the aim, but his paradigm can today be understood more broadly than Freud himself was able to. A discussion of perversion shows that psychoanalysis has moved from seeing it as defensive against instinctual derivatives to seeing it as defensive against object-relatedness. This reflects a shift in the analytic conceptualization of sexuality in general. Freud's paradigm for the sexual drive can be reconceived in terms of source, aim and quality of relatedness to object. Such a view of sexuality also has implications for gender issues, for the comparison of male and female perversion, and for the relation between sexuality and love.

Iris and the Friends: A Year of Memories by John Bayley. Published by Duckworth, London, 1999; 208 pages; £16.95

Jennifer Silverstone

Jennifer Silverstone

Jennifer Silverstone  

Iris Murdoch, philosopher and novelist, died on 8 February 1999 three months after her husband John Bayley, himself an academic and author, wrote his first book about her. The second was published immediately after her death. The first book was a bestseller for Duckworth his publishers; the fate of the second is not yet known.

The first of these books begins in a moving and promising way, charting the beginnings of a relationship between the author and Iris that was to lead to a marriage. They remained a childless couple with their exceptional creativity being harnessed into their work. The marriage itself reads for all the world like a haven for two siblings, away from the parental couple. Oblivious of the pain of being behind the bedroom door, they seem to muddle through an enchanted life: a kind of secret world of perpetual latency.

John Bayley conveys the slow decline in ‘Iris's’ mental health with a benevolence and a tolerance which are both illuminating and moving. How does he manage to be himself and stay within himself in the thrall of her mental collapse? In part the explanation seems to rest in the paradox that in her diminished state of mind, and in her consequent absolute dependence on him, he is closer to her as a physical human being than ever before. The disintegration in her mental life leads them into more of what he calls a ‘marriage’, a closeness and physical intimacy that he had not known with her before. There is no longer an otherness in her condition; there is a sameness.

It is a moving and tragic tale made the more so because it was written whilst she was still alive, typed on the typewriter in the early mornings whilst she lay beside him in the marital bed: there and not there, absent and present. She was private and silent. He was private and about to go public. ‘Her reserve was deep and as natural to her as it was deep’ (Bayley 1998, p. 69). But now we know that this fierce intellectual, this author who could be the dreamer of inner worlds and creator of complex others, was fed baked beans and watched The Telly-Tubbies. The infant state within her to which she so determinedly returned revealed the blessing of a warm and benevolent inner self. In Iris Murdoch's case Dr Alzheimer had become a benevolent murderer of the soul, a guide backwards, taking her to regression, into the pre-babbling state of infancy. No rage, violence and uncontrollable states of mind here; at least not too many moments of the sheer terror of being with someone out of control, out of their mind, whose speech is reduced to anguished moans. What Bayley does convey is the sheer tedium, the frustration, of sameness and the helplessness in the face of ‘Iris's’ perpetual call ‘when are we leaving’, and moments of his despair.

This paper surveys the legislative context for the statutory regulation of psychotherapy as in summer 1999. It looks at the public policy of regulation. The Parliamentary progress of the Health Bill (Health Act, as of 30 June 1999) is examined and its successful outcome for professions. The experience of State Registration for a profession is explored and benefits elaborated. The options for how the profession might take up the new opportunities are presented and a timescale indicated.

This is an overview of the topic and cannot attempt to do it justice in detail. Areas such as the history of regulated professions, how educational approvals are conducted, devolution, complaints and conduct procedures and many others will have to be dealt with elsewhere.

The Impossibility of Sex by Susie Orbach. Published by Penguin Books, London, 1999; 216 pages; £17.99 hardback

James Taylor

James Taylor

James Taylor  

Somewhere between received wisdom and hackneyed cliché lies the old adage ‘one should not judge a book by its cover’; a common-place sentiment so apparently sound that it hardly seems worth reflecting upon. Yet it is right here that we might begin. The object, in its lay sense, is a hard-backed book, on the red side of pink, emblazoned in its middle with The Impossibility of Sex. Covering this, like a grey skin, is a dust-jacket depicting the back of a woman's head and the legend ‘Susie Orbach’. (Exactly whose head is never revealed, though the author's would be a fair guess.) Cut into the centre of this head is a small square hole, perhaps discovering what's at the back of this therapist's mind and, then, perhaps not. My equivocation relates to the curious demands The Impossibility of Sex places upon the reader, falling as it does between the known genres of metapsychological primers, case histories and collections of short stories. Indeed, it is as if this ‘generic straddling’ is signed by the physical fact of the book long before we realize that the preponderance of what follows is an analyst thinking about a made-up therapist thinking about made-up clients. However, the book is so much more than this. The narrative layering reminiscent of The Canterbury Tales or, say, the novels of Henry James is there to further Orbach's endeavour to remove the shrouds of secrecy that have surrounded psychoanalysis for years and to ‘make an authentic representation of feeling states’ (p. 197), particularly those of the working therapist. The irony of wearing a mask in order to tell a truth is not lost on the author, who does not attempt to perform the intriguing if unethical feat of rendering ‘What really goes on in the therapist's consulting room’, as the press release merrily trumpets. Instead, with deconstructive insight into the case history, she points out that it was ever thus as, through the necessary acts of ‘selection and concealment’ (p. 194), a distortion and fiction are always made of who the patient is. Even professional literature depends upon artifice.

Small is Beautiful

Maggie Fagan

Maggie Fagan

Maggie Fagan  

I'm going to talk about the issues of scale whilst considering how we work at the Arbours Crisis Centre. At the Centre we have three groups of people, three resident therapists, six guests (the name we give to our patients at the Centre) and 10 team leaders.

The guests who come to the Centre are extremely damaged people. They live on a precipice, their identities uncertain, unsure whether they want to live - or not. Many of our guests over recent years have inhabited the borderline state of mind, neither in relationships nor out of them, ‘stable in their instability’ (Fonagy 1991), neither choosing life nor death but often finding frightening behaviours that keep them compromised at death's door. Many of the guests at the Centre ‘do’ something destructive like bingeing or cutting. Usually they are people who in their history have experienced someone ‘doing’ something to them - they have been intruded upon by others. Their ‘no’, perhaps in a situation of abuse, has not been heard. Consequently as part of their way of communicating they ‘do’ things to themselves… and to others, usually through the launching of violent projections - that is, forcing their anxieties into other people. For people in this borderline state of mind nothing is right, and, often, despite having used considerable energy to get to the Crisis Centre, when they get there, everything is wrong. The food is wrong, the rooms are too big or too small, the resident therapists are either always too busy when you want them, or they are knocking on your door just when you wanted to be alone. Rooms are too hot or too cold, team leaders are either too removed, or too demanding on the guest - and so on. This is the borderline world where the world of intimate relations between subject and object, mother and child, has been profoundly damaged. And there is the longing for the transformational object - the perfect person or place that will make everything right.

Often, guests at the Centre experience a crisis on arriving (Berke 1987) for they feel they are going to be trapped in a cruel setting where everything is wrong. They worry that no one will like them, and that no one would voluntarily want to be with them. For these people every attempt must then be made to control others, through projective processes -that is, making other people feel as they feel. ‘The Relationship Place’

Lois Elliott

Lois Elliott

Lois Elliott  

As many of you know the Arbours Crisis Centre is a unique place. The previous papers have told you something about our work and our ideology, which is what makes us unique. The most important aspect of this is our ability to develop relationships. In her paper Cath discussed the resident therapists' ability to establish relationships with the guests, while Maggie pointed out the importance of this relationship as well as the one between the resident therapists and the team leaders.

This is what our work is about. It is through relationships that we gain the satisfaction of knowing that we have been able to help someone. But the opportunity for this to happen can only occur because of the relationship which the guests allow us to build with them.

For many of the people who come to the Crisis Centre for help, this special relationship is one in which they are the main participant: where they can talk, they can be heard and where they wish to understand and be understood. This is an experience which they may not have had for a long time, often never. As Joe said in his introduction, ‘therapeutic healing lies in calm, containing, considerate and considered relationships’. But more than this, through their experience at the Centre, guests are able to find more of themselves. They can, as Joe went on to say, ‘serve as effective helpers both to new guests and to the resident therapists’, thereby finding a value and worth in what they themselves can give, and a renewed belief in the vitality of relationships.

Relationships are the mainstay of the Crisis Centre, but not only relationships within the Centre itself. There are many other relationships that have nurtured, nourished and sustained the Centre over its 25 years, starting at the beginning with the relationship between Joseph Berke and Morton Schatzman. Our relationship with the other Arbours facilities and with our Trustees has given us advice and support. Laurie Slade

Laurie Slade

71 Netheravon Road, London W4 2NB

Laurie Slade  

Reading this neatly typed and orderly presentation of Brian's story, I feel inhibited from marking or underlining the passages which interest me - from making a mess of the pages. Separately, I cover my notepad with a mess of unconnected responses. Brian's conflicted presence is powerfully evoked.

I'm gripped by Brian's story as it unfolds, and feel that therapist and client are equally gripped. Their therapeutic alliance seems well established. Despite the sense of stuckness, the work seems alive. The therapist is able to think during a session, aware of countertransference experiences, moving between analytic reflection and spontaneous involvement. I feel emboldened to exercise a similar freedom - while remaining aware that reverie of this kind cannot amount to an interpretation, since it does not form part of an ongoing dialogue.

The therapist's unanswered questions are important - not for what the answers might be, but because they show the therapist struggling with the messiness of not knowing. I am strongly tempted to order my notes, to begin theorizing about the material. I feel I must stay with my own unanswered questions.

Brian started therapy when he was doing his course, and his therapy seems a bit like his coursework. He gives himself assignments - to visualize, fantasize, think what he really wants. Intellectualizing his therapy may be helping him to remain with the therapy, but is it getting in the way?

Cognitive Analytic Therapy and Borderline Personality Disorder: The Model and the Method by Anthony Ryle. Published by John Wiley & Sons, Chichester, 1997; 187 pages; £34.95 hardback, £16.99 paperback.

Lawrence Welch

Lawrence Welch

Leeds

Lawrence Welch  

The questions, of whether the concept of Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) is ‘real’, how it develops, whether it is treatable and by what methods, are becoming defining features of many psychotherapies. While accepting the problems with the DSM-IV diagnosis, Ryle argues that ‘there is no diagnostic system which offers an alternative and more satisfactory method’ (p. 4). He powerfully summarizes the social causes of BPD while at the same time identifying how those with BPD maintain their past experiences:

The predominant source of borderline patients' difficulties is the experience of cruelty and neglect; in most cases they have had little or no trustworthy, predictable care and they have usually suffered physical or sexual abuse from at least one parent. The result is that they tend to repeat what they know, accepting and inflicting on self and others the neglect and abuse which was their constant experience. (p. 35)

He argues for a relatively short-term treatment (about 24 sessions with follow-ups) as a good first offer to patients who are often regarded as beyond treatment or as requiring an impractically long and intensive therapy. His book provides an intellectually rigorous overview of the concept of BPD with a critical analysis of the competing accounts of this diagnosis and therapies addressing it.

As a Cognitive Analytic Therapist (CAT) myself I have to confess to a partisan view. The offer of the review elicited within me the desire to read the book intensively rather than focusing on chapters. I was surprised to find I struggled to follow my ‘cover to cover’ purpose. As I reflected on this difficulty, I felt it was centrally tied up with a reaction to the pain contained in the stories given in the book. The list of DSMIV's nine traits, including unstable interpersonal relationships, frantic efforts to avoid abandonment, suicidal and self-mutilating behaviour, indicate clearly the forms of distress this group experience. What the list cannot adequately convey is the impact of the stories they have to tell. The trauma, abuse, cruelty and neglect expressed in the stories are unfortunately all too familiar in clinical practice in the NHS, but familiarity does not lessen the effect of reading the narratives of these men and women.

Commentary by a Psychoanalytical Phenomenological Psychotherapist

Mary Ellis

Mary Ellis

London N7 OEG

Mary Ellis  

Although the therapist does not explicitly outline the purpose of her presentation of her work with Brian in her introduction, my impression is that she is keen to engage with other perspectives which might throw light on her intense feelings of frustration in her relationship with him and her experience of how ‘so often in our sessions we seem to be going round and round, getting nowhere’. It is in this spirit that I want to address the questions that arise for me in reading this case presentation.

I would have welcomed more directly reported speech of the patient throughout the presentation as I am often unsure whether the language is that of the patient or that of the therapist. For example, did Brian say he had ‘repressed’ his sexuality or is this the therapist's word? Are the descriptions of his mother as ‘dominant and forceful’ and his father as ‘ineffectual’ the therapist's or Brian's? The contribution of phenomenological thought to the practice of psychotherapy is primarily its emphasis on the description of experiences rather than on an explanation of them. This allows for greater attention to the uniqueness of the patient's world, consciously and unconsciously, whether conveyed in the languages of images, words or embodiment. In this case, since a central struggle for Brian is the question of how to be alive and separate from his parents, a sensitivity on the part of the therapist to the individuality of his own language would be especially crucial to the work.

The therapist goes on to interpret the relations between the parents as ‘a very disparate internalized parental couple’. The concept of the ‘internalized parental couple’ is, I think, restrictive since it is underpinned by particular views of normality and pathology. My interest would be in what the specific dynamics between Brian's intrusive mother and his ineffectual father meant for Brian.

[[RunningHead]]

Introduction to the Celebration**

Joseph Berke

Joseph Berke

Joseph Berke  

The 25th anniversary is a very important occasion in the life of the Centre, which was founded by myself and others in the spring of 1973. This means we are actually 26 years old today - but who's counting? I am very pleased to greet everyone connected with us, including members of our Professional Advisory Committee, as well as colleagues, trainees and trustees. Also I would like to extend warm greetings to old friends and new friends, and especially our guests of honour tonight, Professor Robert Hinshelwood, whose help and guidance have been so important over many years, and Sir Louis Blom-Cooper, who has contributed greatly to the field of mental health.

We established the Crisis Centre in order to offer intensive, personal, psychological and social support to individuals and families in severe emotional distress. Equally important, we wanted our interventions to reflect kindness and humanity as well as psychological acuity. We wanted to respond to people at a time of pain and instability in their lives with respect. And we wanted to be sensitive to their social relations and to be concerned for their experience, that is, their subjectivity, as well as behaviour, their objective reality.

When adults and children are upset, they may be overwhelmed with dis-ease, but not necessarily disease. A friendly ear to hear hurt, a shoulder to cry on, an attentive eye to see what is going on, and a containing mind to make sense of muddle, are at least as useful, if not more useful, than conventional psychobiological treatments. We thought and, indeed, still think that therapeutic magic or healing power lies in calm, containing, considerate and considered relationships, rather than pills, shock, institutionalization or physical restraint.

As I described in our original brochure, we intended and still intend that the Centre should be a sanctuary, an oasis in an emotional wilderness, a place where people can contain and make sense of their experiences, and achieve a renewed sense of integrity and autonomy.

[[RunningHead]]

Response to Jeremy Holmes

Isobel Hunter-Brown

Isobel Hunter-Brown

Isobel Hunter-Brown  

In response to the article ‘NHS Psychotherapy - past, future and present’ by Jeremy Holmes (BJP 16(4): 447-457), I would like to add a footnote.

This is in the form of an amendment as regards the story of psychotherapy in Scotland. Holmes rightly mentions the long tradition in psychotherapy in Edinburgh and Aberdeen. No mention is made of Glasgow, which from 1920 had the first Child Guidance Clinic in Scotland, and in 1938, like Edinburgh, began an outpatient psychotherapy clinic for neurotics (the Lansdowne). Both were taken over by the NHS. In the mid-50s Glasgow was the more active NHS psychotherapy centre. The Professor of Psychiatry in Glasgow employed a fully qualified psychoanalyst, Dr Tom Freeman, in 1952 to assist with training of junior psychiatrists in psychoanalytic psychotherapy. Freeman later became Director of the Lansdowne Clinic and had other psychoanalysts on his staff. He wrote an article in the British Journal of Psychiatry (Freeman 1967), presenting the results in 33 cases of individual psychoanalytic psychotherapy and 95 treated with group psychotherapy.

The culture of mental hospitals in Scotland, from their inception in the nineteenth century generally tended to be more human than was common in the South and there was some practice of individual psychodynamic psychotherapy in Glasgow Royal Mental Hospital, Gartnavel, in the 1950s. Dr Freeman was also employed there and had sessions too as psychotherapy supervisor from time to time in the Professorial Unit in Dundee and at the Crighton Royal Hospital in Dumfries. The latter hospital, during World War II, had on its staff psychoanalysts who were refugees from Hitler's Germany.

Even the small hospital, Dingleton, near Melrose, had psychotherapeutic input as was shown in the 1960s with the introduction of therapeutic community measures by Maxwell Jones, an Edinburgh graduate with much psychoanalytic background. He had earlier pioneered therapeutic community work in Belmont Hospital near London (later Henderson Hospital).

Dear Editor

I am writing to ask if you would be willing to mention in your Journal a new initiative being undertaken by the University of Hertfordshire and Jessica Kingsley Publishers. We are developing a series of short books on research and innovation in the Arts Therapies. We hope to enable a wide variety of people to publish their ideas and analysis of their work on research. Hence, we would like to invite readers and contributors to your Journal to take part.

The Arts Therapies Research Library (ATRL) series is a joint venture between the University of Hertfordshire and Jessica Kingsley Publishers. It is essentially an anthology of innovative and/or challenging essays on research and aims to develop the range and scope of the Arts Therapies and their neighbouring disciplines by creating a forum for discovery and debate. The series aims to publish between three and four books a year, each on a theme. Psychotherapy Research10(2), 147-158, 2000

Self-Image and Perception of Mother and Father in Psychotic and Borderline Patients

Kerstin Armelius and Ake Granberg

Psychotic and borderline patients rated their self-image and their perception of their mother and father using the Structural Analysis of Social Behavior model (SASB). The borderline patients had more negative images of themselves and their parents, especially their fathers, than did the psychotic patients and the normal subjects, while the psychotic patients' ratings did not differ much from those of the normal subjects. The self-image was related to the images of both parents for borderline patients and normal subjects, while for the psychotic patients only the image of the mother was important for the self-image. In addition, the psychotic patients did not differentiate between the poles of control and autonomy in the introjected self-image. It was concluded that borderline patients are characterized by negative attachment, while psychotic patients are characterized by poor separation from the mother and poor differentiation between autonomy and control. The paper also discusses how this may influence the patients' relations to others.



Psychotherapy Research10(2), 159-168, 2000

Motivation to Seek Psychotherapy in Patients with Recurrent Depressive Disorder

Peter H. Vetter, Joachim v. Pritzbuer, Karl Jungmann, Hans W. Moises, Peter Kropp and Olaf Koller

Fifty-five hospital-treated patients with the ICD-10 diagnosis of recurrent depressive episode(s) were classified according to the Newcastle Depressive Diagnostic Scale as having either psychogenic (n = 25) or endogenous (n = 30) depression and interviewed using the Composite International Diagnostic Interview and the Questionnaire for Assessment of Motivation to Seek Psychotherapy. The two groups were found to differ significantly from one another in two Motivation to Seek Psychotherapy subscales (‘layman's etiology’ and ‘general expectations from therapy’). The motivation to seek psychotherapy was greater in patients with psychogenic depression than in patients with endogenous depression. Nonetheless, psychotherapy is indispensable in treating endogenous depression, especially for patients under situational stress or at risk of suicide.

N. Temple

N. Temple

London

N. Temple  

Dear Editor

Thank you for your letter of 11 June inviting us to reply to Mr Don Feasey's letter.

I'm sorry that Mr Feasey did not receive a response to his original letter, which objected strongly to the television programmes. I think this was due to the large response we had to the programmes.

It is true that the decision to make programmes about the clinical work of the Tavistock was not an easy one. A great deal of thought was given to this decision within the Clinic. At length it was decided that it was possible to find an appropriate and ethical way of making a series of programmes about assessments in psychotherapy and family therapy. We did not feel it would be possible to make programmes about ongoing psychotherapy without disrupting the process. We believed that, by allowing a full discussion with the patients involved and seeking their permission for all the material that was shown, it was possible to give them an opportunity to make a genuine decision about their involvement in the programmes.

I do not agree with Mr Feasey's assertion that the patients involved were unable to give informed consent. In fact the patients felt that what was shown of their interviews in the programmes was respectful of them, and also they felt that others might benefit from their experience. Both the Tavistock clinicians and the BBC team gave a lot of time and thought to enable them to make the decision with full regard to the consequences. In the first place the patients had responded to an advertisement which indicated that the BBC was making a programme about the Tavistock's work. In several cases they felt that this gave them the opportunity to find help that they did not believe was easily available to them. The patients formed a strong positive link to the BBC, which had to be taken into account in the clinical work.

We felt that the programmes were a serious attempt to demonstrate how psychotherapy and family therapy take place, and that the producers of the series, Beth Holgate and Ines Cavill, understood the importance of portraying the work in depth and with respect for the patients and clinicians involved.

F.H. Balfour  

In order to begin the process that might lead eventually to the statutory regulation of psychotherapists, agreement will have to be reached between the mentalhealth disciplines and the psychotherapy institutions on a structure that can contain and govern the profession. Commentary by a Systemic Psychotherapist

Jenny Altschuler

Jenny Altschuler

120 Belsize Lane, London NW3

Jenny Altschuler  

This was a very brave and painful account of the experience of working with a family at a transitional point in their lives. Drawing on systemic theory and practice, alternative ways of understanding the material will be introduced. However, it is important to recognize that these comments are based on what has been written only. Inevitably, we all choose from a range of options in constructing any narrative of our experience, and it may well be that some of what is discussed has been considered by the authors, but has not been addressed in this paper.

Commenting, firstly, on the level of theory, systemic work focuses primarily on the interaction between family members and/or family and therapist. In drawing on the interplay between container and contained (Bion 1962) the authors highlight a connection with a central aspect of systemic family therapy, that the experience of one person is intimately connected with their relationship to others within their intimate system. However, while Bion focuses on what is happening at an internal intrapsychic level, systems theory attends more to what is happening at an interpersonal level, in the relationship between people.

Emphasis is placed on the family as a psychological entity, where the response of one family member is intimately connected with the response of others.

Developmental vs. Social Personality Models of Adult Attachment and Mental ILL Health

trauma, sexual abuse, abusive therapy, perversion

This paper reviews recent literature pertaining to therapists who sexually exploit their clients. It examines some of the common characteristics that have been identified in therapists who abuse, and the psychosexual factors in their background. It goes on to discuss the dynamics which may prevail in the event of therapist abuse. Research suggests that therapists who exploit their role will only do so if they are in some way dysfunctional (Russell 1993). Similarly, therapists who abuse are found to have severe problems with their own sexual identities and experience a considerable amount of sexual anxiety and guilt in their personal relationships (Strean 1993b). It is suggested that their own unresolved conflicts take precedence over those of their clients and unconsciously they harbour a deep antipathy towards the practice of psychotherapy (Strean 1993a).

Giovanna Di Ceglie  

The play Six Characters in Search of an Author is about madness, its seductiveness, its at times apparent plausibility, its language and its infectiousness. It makes the spectator participate in a psychotic experience. A great deal of disturbance in the audience followed its first performance in 1920 at the Teatro la Valle in Rome. By representing what is ultimately the failure of mental and theatrical representation Pirandello has created a work of art which is a most interesting anticipation and validation of the work on psychotic states of mind of the last few decades. In this paper we explore aspects of the play which are relevant to the work in the consulting room with a group of psychotic or borderline patients whose functioning is evocative of the Six Characters in Search of an Author.

[[RunningHead]]

Prescript

Helen Robinson

Helen Robinson

Helen Robinson  

This lecture was given as part of a day of lectures and discussions on ‘Beckett/Bion: The Emergence of Meaning’, a day set up by the Lincoln Clinic and Centre for Psychotherapy and held at University College London in September 1999. The lectures were held alongside a viewing of Samuel Beckett's play Endgame which was part of the Barbican Beckett Festival, brought by the Gate Theatre, Dublin, and was a showing of major works of all kinds by the author. The lecture was conceived as a talk

and relates to the performance of Endgame which the participants would have had the chance to see. Although now published in written and not spoken form this text has retained much of the format of a talk, an interaction with the audience in the tradition of Freud and his early lectures on psychoanalysis, in the hope that this format might apprehend the processes of mind that obtain in the analytic/self-analytic process. The latter traditionally seeks a way towards meanings less than conscious, by means of an oral dialogue, a two-person process, this being what essentially facilitates the kind of knowledge psychoanalysis pursues. The more traditional paper, which Freud also used, the scientific format, has been deliberately eschewed as a less satisfactory medium for demonstrating the presence and use of unconscious process, the latter being the results of findings, the theoretical positioning, as against the dialogic enquiry which is a condensed, fragmentary and processive form. These, therefore, in this talk, are not findings, but demonstrate the satisfactions and dissatisfactions of the way towards finding (pursuits of mind), and do so by what are traditionally poetic means, rhythm, imagery, condensation, symbolization, repetition, alliteration and all manner of rhetoric to please and persuade the listener towards the meanings that words are capable of under the intense constraints of conscious and unconscious concentration on meaning, the emergence of meaning.

The talk addresses the kinds ofmeaning Beckett and Bion illuminate in their different disciplines, Art and Psychoanalysis, and assumes in the choice of their dialogues with us, both Beckett and Bion, that the unconscious processes and their difficult presence in conscious life are of significance and concern to all. The emphasis by Beckett and Bion on the failure of expression as the paradoxical centrality of expression is explored with its relevance to all psychodynamic processes, those of the theatre of Beckett (with Shakespeare before him) and those of the theatre of Bion (with Freud before him).

The Statutory Registration of Psychotherapy

Ann Casement

Ann Casement

UKCP. 167-169 Great Portland Street, London WIN 5FB. [e-mail: ukcp@psychotherapy.org.uk]

Ann Casement  

Lord Alderdice, the Liberal Democrat Peer and Speaker to the Northern Irish Assembly, met with Ann Casement, Chair of the UK Council for Psychotherapy, in February 1999 at the House of Lords and offered to bring a Private Member's Bill to regulate the profession of psychotherapy. They subsequently met with the then Minister for Health in the Lords, Baroness Hayman, and Anne Richardson, Senior Policy Adviser to the Department of Health. At this meeting, Lord Alderdice presented the case for taking the regulation of psychotherapists through a Private Member's Bill route because many psychotherapists do not work in the NHS. The draft psychotherapy Bill is being put forward to regulate the private sector as there are a range of ways in which the public are protected in the public sector. For this reason, he feels that the two possible routes open to regulation under the Health Act are not suitable for psychotherapy. One of these routes would be under Schedule 3 of the Act, which allows for new professions to become regulated, and the other is the new regulation for the Council for Professions Supplementary to Medicine (CPSM) to be renamed the Health Professions Council, which regulates professions primarily working in the NHS e.g. physiotherapists and radiographers.

Lord Alderdice called a meeting on the 22 October 1999 at the House of Lords of eight of the professional bodies in the psychotherapy field to discuss his proposed draft Psychotherapy Bill. The content of the Bill states that there be put in place a General Psychotherapy Council with an elected Chair. This General Council would be made up of members of the psychotherapy profession but at least half its membership would consist of lay members such as Privy Councillors. There would also be a Registrar to establish and maintain a central Register of psychotherapists.

The Bill would also put in place an Education Committee which would have the duty of promoting high standards of training in psychotherapy. Further, there would be a Code of Practice which would lay down standards of conduct and practice that would be expected of registered psychotherapists. Linked to this, there would be a Health Committee, a Professional Conduct Committee and an Investigating Committee which would look into allegations against a psychotherapist and have the power to impose conditions with which a psychotherapist must comply. Finally, there would be a system of appeals which can be brought to the General Council against decisions made by the Registrar, Health Committee or Professional Conduct Committee.

Changing Aims in Psychoanalysis

Anna Dreher

Anna Dreher

Keplerstrasse 22, D60318 Frankfurt am Main, Germany

Anna Dreher  

About the Problem of the Treatment Aim

It is probably not so difficult to answer the question of what aims one has upon entering therapy; or what aims we ourselves have when we are patients - it is more difficult with the therapists. I would like to elucidate the subject from this perspective, and ask what are the aims of psychoanalysts. Spontaneously, one could answer: analysts, like other people, too, want to earn money and live happily. And although I am, in this paper, mainly dealing with those specific aims which analysts have when they practise their profession - that is, when they analyse patients - I shall nonetheless devote later on just a little time to the topics of happiness and money.

In the last decade, there has been a growing demand worldwide that the effectiveness of our analytic method be proven. Whoever - psychotherapists or outcome researchers - defines treatment aims, and then wishes to determine whether these aims have been met, is forced to name the respective criteria. For psychotherapy research, which today is mainly quantitative-empirical research, it would of course be desirable to have criteria which are easy to measure. But measuring is a difficult task in psychoanalysis. Its subject matter is too resistive, the influencing variables are too manifold and, what is more, we are talking about changes of the inner world, with particular emphasis on its unconscious components.

When formulating these criteria for treatment aims (such as the modification of the superego), reference is of course made to psychoanalytic concepts, like transference, the depressive position or the superego. Concepts are immensely important; they constitute our view of the world, and they provide us with categories by which we organize the phenomena that interest us. In psychoanalysis - which, in Freud's words, is ‘feeling its way forwards on an empirical basis’ (Freud 1919, p. 210) - a lot of knowledge has been condensed in our concepts, and these concepts in turn have been determining our therapeutic procedures.

Editorial

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale  

The concept of the mirror has been considered indispensable to psychotherapists in the quest for the therapeutic discovery of the self, but what aspect of mirroring is needed or meant when so many different uses of the term are available? The pool as the mirror for Narcissus, the joy in the mother's face for Winnicott, or perhaps Lacan's mirror stage when the child gives up his interiority? In the ‘concept of mind’ literature the mirror refers to attunement and reflection, to finding in the analyst's functioning mind the discovery by the patient of a mind of his own; in group analysis the mirror has to do with the discovery of unconscious parts of the self in the group mirror, and so on. In their article on Pirandello's play Six Characters in Search of an Author, Domenico and Giovanna Rita Di Ceglie find parallels to the analytic experience of a particular kind of mirroring with borderline patients. Patients who have had insufficient experience of containment express a need for mirroring of the sort that adds or subtracts nothing, that gives back exactly what is communicated. In this, there is a demand that projective identifications are held unaltered and uninterpreted, repeating identically the original experience, similarly to Pirandello's characters who cannot represent but only repeat or re-enact their story, blurring fiction and reality, leading to the chaos of madness. Helping the more disturbed patients to allow a shared, elaborated meaning and language, a triadic space that allows for real communication and symbol formation, is the process that in the play ends in failure. Pirandello and the Di Ceglies are acutely aware that we must not take for granted that words communicate or have a mutually agreed meaning, as psychotic aspects of the person often alter the meaning according to a private language of his/her own.

The talking cure in relation to schizophrenia has had a chequered past and a present in which there is disagreement and debate. The ‘Conversational Model’ of therapy devised by Robert Hobson was applied to two seriously disturbed and treatmentresistant psychiatric inpatients on a community-type ward. The ‘Conversational Model’ is described, as is the treatment of the two patients and the outcome, which shows symptom improvement on problem behaviour scales.

Response to Jackie Gerrard

Warren Colman

Warren Colman

Warren Colman  

I would like to make a few comments on Jackie Gerrard's very interesting article, ‘Ocnophilia and the interpretation of transference’ (BJP 16(4): 400-411).

I do not think there is really such a great difference in approach between Gerrard and Balint, but what is most encouraging about Gerrard's views and her account of her own clinical practice is that they show just how much analysis has moved on since 1968. It seemed to me that the reason Gerrard found herself disagreeing with Balint was because his idea of what constituted a transference interpretation was probably very different from current ideas and practice. In the Balint example she quoted, I would have thought that what Balint said to his patient was a transference interpretation, albeit it was couched in the form of giving his reasons for not acceding to the patient's request for an extra session. He seemed to think that transference interpretations were purely directed to unconscious libidinal drives and therefore bypassed the patient's actual need of the therapist. In the language of self-psychology, Balint's objection was to interpretations which are ‘experience-distant’ at a point when what the patient needs above all is recognition of their need in the moment. This kind of recognition was precisely what Gerrard's own clinical examples demonstrated.

In her first example, it was not only through interpretation but also through her action of offering an extra session that the patient felt held and understood. (There are interesting issues about the frame here: was the extra session that Gerrard offered different from the one Balint's patient requested because it was a regular session - and thus an extension of the frame rather than a breaking of it - or is there some inherent difference between a Thursday session and a weekend session? Perhaps our ideas about the sacrosanct nature of weekends have also changed since 1968?) Throughout the article, Gerrard argues sensitively and with great warmth of feeling for the acceptance and recognition of the patient's need to cling, held in balance with the need to interpret the underlying anxieties behind it. In other words, Gerrard's interpretations are based, not on libidinal drive theory, but on a recognition of the patient's actual need for the therapist and the centrality of holding and containment to the therapeutic process. Both her actions and her interpretations are directed at providing that holding and containment.

WatchingLolita (directed by Adrian Lyne, 1997)

Fiona Gardner

Fiona Gardner

Fiona Gardner  

In the 1950s and 1960s Lolita became a word synonymous with a sexually precocious pre-adolescent girl, for Lolita made Lolita more famous than her creator, the author, Vladimir Nabokov. The book was first published in 1955 though not until 1959 in this country, and in 1958 was made into a film. A second version made in the more knowing culture of the late 1990s went on general release, and is a careful though disappointing interpretation.

The story is as much a matter of kidnap, sexual abuse and coercion as the absorbing passion of a lost enamoured soul, although the story appears to belong to Humbert Humbert, a paedophile and poet obsessed with ‘nymphets’. He travels from Europe to America and develops a terrible passion for the young daughter of his landlady. Circumstances lead him to the position of stepfather, widower and then sole guardian of the girl, and they travel back and forth across America staying together in motel rooms. After two years Lolita escapes from him with another paedophile and pornographer called Quilty -Humbert's ‘guilty’ doppelganger or alter ego. Three years pass before Humbert finds Lolita, now pregnant and married to a poor young man. Humbert murders the paedophile/ pornographer who took her from him, and writes the story from his prison cell. At the end of the film we are told that both died, Humbert in his cell and Lolita in childbirth.

The effect of watching the film was unsettling, much more so than reading the book; therefore following the contemporary injunction ‘Only deconstruct’, I would like to disentangle my after-thoughts. This then is hardly a film review, but that may be in keeping with Nabokov's book, the second title of which, The Confession of a White Widowed Male, is a parody both of a psychiatric or psychoanalytic case study and of a titillating confessional novel, raising the expectations of the reader who hopes the book will provide the pleasures of pornography. Inevitably the book's reputation among non-readers is of a pornographic novel but, while the first part of the book is often erotic, Nabokov withholds explicit sexual descriptions.

Group Therapy: Group-Analytic Psychotherapy with the Elderly

Maria Canete , Fiona Stormont and Arturo Ezquerro

Arturo Ezquerro

57 Hamlet Square, London NW2 1SR

Arturo Ezquerro  

Orthodox psychoanalysis offered the view that mental processes in the elderly are too rigidly established for favourable treatment results. Group psychotherapy with the elderly in general has received little attention, mostly concentrating on inpatient groups. The main focus has been on supportive techniques, often in institutional settings.

Two of the authors (Maria Canete and Fiona Stormont) co-conducted a weekly slow-open analytic group for elderly people, in a London outpatient NHS clinic. This paper presents clinical material that illustrates some age-specific issues, as they appear in the group process. For example, issues of competitiveness, rivalry and aggression, which are generally present in the beginning of groups with younger people, tend to be absent, or manifest themselves differently, in the elderly group. Denial of age becomes impossible, which helps these patients to accept approaching death and the process of dying itself. Psychoanalytic group psychotherapy can be especially indicated for this age population.

Correspondence

Dear Editor

I was concerned to read Susannah Izzard's article ‘Oedipus - baby or bathwater?’ in the Autumn number of 1999 (BJP 16(1)). I understand her to view psychoanalysis as including explanations of the cause of homosexuality, as attributing homosexuality as pathological and as having failed to update the Oedipus complex in the light of the variety of family and social systems now recognized. I would like to touch on some concerns I have about each of these points as much as space allows.

Psychoanalytic attributions of cause seem to me to be no longer a part of metapsychological thought. The causal explanations which she quotes have a quaintness which makes it difficult for me to take them seriously as the basis of a heuristic endeavour. I think it is tactful to ignore such formulations. Were psychoanalysis a predictive science its status would be quite different. Sadly, we can only try to help patients to understand their difficulties in bearing the pain of reality. We cannot tell them how such difficulties arose.

So far has psychoanalysis gone from historical explanation that accounts of psychodynamics today tend to be accounts of psychic reality. We may speculate as to how parental handling contributed to the organization of that psychic reality, but such speculations have little part in modern technique. Psychoanalysis now deals with the situation as it is without regard for how it arose, just as the fire service might attend an incident according to the type of fire and not at all according to whether or not it was set deliberately. We might wish for a predictive psychoanalysis but we do not have one. It therefore seems to me needless to consider psychoanalytic explanations of homosexuality when we do not consider explanations of any other developmental anomalies.

As to homosexuality being anomalous, clearly a statement implying pathology, homosexuality can easily be considered an anomaly of biological development. As such it may have evolutionary advantages like the sterility of worker bees and ants but that is a matter for biology, for a discipline within zoology of human ethology. Susannah Izzard herself gives moving documentation of Freud's defence of the social rights of homosexuals and of his distinction of the inversion of object choice from the perversion of drive. The documents she quotes suggest that the culture of psychoanalysis has hardly kept up with Freud's humanity nor with his scientific honesty regarding our ignorance about homosexuality.

Commentary by a Psychiatrist, Sexual and Couple Therapist

Michael Crowe

Michael Crowe

Michael Crowe  

This is an interesting and clinically impressive account of short-term family and couple therapy. The description of the clinical sessions is convincing, and the family comes to life in the account in a way which suggests that the therapists both liked and helped them. In addition, the therapists are not afraid to use everyday descriptions of the family's behaviour and interaction, a fact which again brings a vividness to their account and allows those of a non-psychoanalytic background to appreciate what was being done.

Oddly, there are some rather imprecise aspects to the detailed information given: father is ‘probably’ in his early 50s, and mother ‘of a similar age’, while the number of sessions of therapy is never clearly stated, although we can infer from internal evidence that it was probably three sessions of family therapy, three sessions of couple therapy and one final session of family therapy. This then was essentially a brief course of therapy, and none the worse for that, but in this respect it contrasts with a great deal of what is commonly believed about psychodynamic couple and family therapy. The usual assumption is that this type of therapy continues for many sessions (Daniell 1985; Clulow 1985). Many analysts would consider a resolution within six sessions to represent either a first stage of therapy, to be followed by the inevitable relapse into depression and need for further therapy, or a ‘flight into health’. There are certainly some forms of ‘brief’ dynamic therapy, but in these one might expect to find some characteristic techniques, such as dealing with issues of termination from the beginning or stressing transference throughout, and they did not seem to have been used; so in many ways it is distinct from the accepted forms of psychoanalytic family therapy.

On the other hand, systemic or cognitive behavioural therapists would applaud the brevity of the therapy and seek for the worthwhile changes which may have taken place in the short time-scale involved. What I intend to do therefore in this comment is to look at the therapy from a different theoretical viewpoint to see if the work of the therapists can be understood in terms other than those they have chosen to interpret it by, and perhaps thereby to point to similarities between psychodynamic and the alternative forms of therapy available.

Face to Face: Therapy as Ethics by Paul Gordon. Published by Constable, London, 1999; 190 pages; £15.99 hardback

Philip Hewitt

Philip Hewitt

Beckenham, Kent

Philip Hewitt  

Although Paul Gordon has not claimed this directly, Face to Face is a book for all psychotherapists. This book is the assembly of a core ethical and theoretical position and unavoidably addresses some difficult questions about the current state of psychotherapy. Whilst Gordon is as suspicious of ‘caring’ (p. 21) as he is of the ‘odour of sanctimony’ (p. 21) as motive forces in psychotherapy, this is a book about ethics, morals and sharing responsibility for what is happening around us in a fast and inexorably changing professional climate. In this sense it is a book with great care for the practice of psychotherapy.

It is not a book of clinical or just theoretical material but, as Gordon says, he has drawn upon all his experience as a therapist and this important work is carefully and sensitively informed by it. It is an ethical statement implicating the subjective commitment of the author to his work. The illusive object of psychotherapy is the subject of discussion. It is a problem which the author admits he does not offer as a direct question because he fears misinterpretation. The misinterpretation is that he would be misunderstood as saying what psychotherapy is rather than inviting the individual to discover for himself how he might be ‘Face to Face’ in a psychotherapeutic relationship, and by this he means something real, meaningful and essentially human. He does not eschew the couch but, inspired by the work of Emmanuel Levinas, he is making another point. The Face is the epiphany of the individual, the unique, at first optical connection with another human being which establishes an inalienable relatedness to the world of human beings. Gordon adumbrates the Levinasian convictions of human responsibility as a priori to the concerns superimposed by training and professional status.

A theme of this book suggests that we have lost our way with preoccupations about power and colonizing information and knowledge. Gordon cites an example of the rebuke handed out by the British Psycho-Analytical Society when the Lacanians also decided to call themselves psychoanalysts (p. 25). This theme of appropriation of knowledge and status is also discussed in terms of the ‘The Will to Science’ (p. 26) ‘The (Pseudo) Medicalization of Therapy)’ (p. 30), ‘The Lure of Professionalism’ (p. 33) and ‘The Tyranny of Theory’ (p. 37). All of this is what he argues is wrong with psychotherapy and what is needed is a new encounter with philosophy, ‘with ideas about ideas, thoughts about thinking, particularly what happens in a room when two individuals meet - or at least try to’ (p. 45).

Circular Reflections: Selected Papers on Group Analysis and Psychoanalysis by Malcolm Pines. Published by Jessica Kingsley, London and Philadelphia, 1998; 240 pages; £17.95 paperback

Herb Hahn

Herb Hahn

London

Herb Hahn  

In this volume, Malcolm Pines reflects his well-earned stature as an erudite scholar, editor of many books and of the Journal of Group Analysis, experienced psychoanalyst and eldest son of group analysis. The book contains a selection of published papers, many of which were originally given as key lectures to a range of national and international analytic organizations. Although arranged in Sections

367

(Group Analysis, Psychoanalysis and Psychotherapy, Historical Perspectives), the chapters overlap creatively in that the author re-turns from many angles to exploring the ‘self’ in relation to early development including mirroring and coherence, the key role of empathy, attunement and dialogue, the echoing of history, and the ubiquity of the socio-psychological. His research, thoughts and penetrating insights encompass individuals, dyads, groups, organizations and society as a whole. While Foulkes and Kernberg are recurrently referred to and engaged with, the text is also illuminated by, and illuminating in relation to, many analytic practitioners, theoreticians and researchers, as well as social scientists, philosophers, poets and writers of fiction.

The first two chapters comprehensively explore and develop the concept of mirroring, particularly in relation to child development. Chapters 3, 4 and 5 consider psychic development and healing in group analysis and its particular application to working with borderline patients. Pines suggests that both psychoanalysis and group analysis strive to replace cohesion (linked to undifferentiation) with coherence (responsible cooperation in a group and ego development in the individual). Group analysis strives for healing, a notion which Freud, unlike Jung, eschewed. In the group, healing relates to the process of developing a sense of ‘wholeness’ which is akin to Jung's concept of individuation.

Regarding analytic work with borderline patients, Pines agrees with Segal about the breakdown of symbol formation, but favours aetiology based on an arrest in development stemming from early disturbed interpersonal relationships. He condemns as a contemporary version of the doctrine of original sin any approach that invokes the notion of constitutional envy in the neonate. In groups, therapeutic work (with not more that one or two borderline patients per group) proceeds in the standard setting. However, the group analyst is wary of the dangers of fragmenting the group by making transference-based group interpretations at the part object level. Individuals are instead shown their place in the pattern of the group as a whole. Support for the group's own efforts to develop is considered essential. Chapter 4 has interesting links with the penultimate chapter of the book, ‘A History of Psychodynamic Psychiatry in Britain’, and the book is worth buying for the fine detail and broad sweep of this chapter alone. The specific links with Chapter 5 relate to the account given of the development and fate of the Bion-inspired approach to Group Psychotherapy at the Tavistock, in contrast to the prolific development of Foulkesian Group Analysis. A broader history of psychodynamic psychology in Britain would include the development of the Bion-related Tavistock Leicester Group Relations Conferences.

Victoria Davenport  

This is an important text that is in danger of being lost on bookshop shelves, partly because of its unhelpful, unimaginative title, and partly because of an insipid cover design (Cupids with bows and arrows), both of which trivialize the serious subject matter within: namely, difficulties that the patient and therapist encounter when confronted with the raw face of intimacy, in whatever form that might take.

374

The book's ten contributors are all well known, and represent a wide spectrum of theoretical stances (two Kleinian, one Lacanian, three Jungian, one Kohutian, and three Independent). There is also an almost equal representation of male (six) and female (four) viewpoints, with no obvious (stereotypical) links between gender and content. Books and papers on this subject seem inevitably (and tiresomely) to present a male therapist who has to contend with his own sexual/erotic feelings and/or those of a female patient; much to its credit, this book accepts the female therapist as equally capable of sexual and erotic feelings towards her patients - male and female - as well as the male therapist as being capable of tender, maternal feelings towards his. The authors accept the inevitability of powerful emotions - regardless of gender - whether on or behind the couch.

The book is divided into three parts, which seem slightly contrived as there is much overlap in subject matter. The titles speak for themselves: Part 1 covers ‘Love and The Erotic: Developmental Issues and Their Relevance to Clinical Practice’ (Jackie Gerrard, Sheila Gordon, Jean Thomson); Part 2, ‘Progressive and Regressive Aspects of the Erotic Transference and Countertransference’ (David Mann, Ronald Doctor, Nathan Field, Martin Stanton, Marco Chiesa); Part 3, ‘Sexual Abuse and Its Impact on Psychotherapy’ (Fiona Gardner, Andrew Samuels, David Mann).

Thorny subjects are tackled in each chapter: for example, Jackie Gerrard confronts the issue that ‘love’ seems to have become a dirty word in our profession: ‘I think it is only when a patient can arouse our deepest loving feelings (not empathy) that we can really hope for a truly positive outcome from our work’ (p. 29); Sheila Gordon takes up the myth of Cupid and Psyche: ‘[the experience of being treated with both care and restraint] is an essential building-block in the development of the mature capacity for loving that the Cupid/Psyche relationship exemplifies’ (p. 51); David Mann confronts the difficulty in allowing unconscious erotic feelings in both the therapist and the patient to emerge; Ronald Doctor gets to the nitty-gritty of ‘defining’, for example, the erotic versus the eroticized transference; Andrew Samuels takes a hard look at ‘safe analysis’: ‘…how, when it is all so real, so infused with physical reality, are the analysing couple going to reach the very symbols and metaphors they are hoping to work with?’ (p. 154), as well as why we may ‘need’ our incestuous feelings.

Editorial

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale  

In the recent debate around Otto Kernberg's paper published on the IJPA website and laying out the differences between psychoanalytic psychotherapy, standard psychoanalysis and supportive analytically-based psychotherapy, most of the email respondents were critical of his three divisions, stating that no such clear-cut differences can be made in practice. All analysts are engaged in all three modalities in the course of an analysis, and several thought that the distinctions made by Kernberg were for political purposes and ‘identity politics’. He called for psychoanalytic training institutions to offer psychoanalytic psychotherapy courses, as this is the modality best suited for more disturbed borderline and other personality disordered patients. Kernberg's paper suggests that psychoanalytic psychotherapy, to the extent it deals with severe identity disturbances, has a special expertise to offer, with wider parameters of technique that differ from standard psychoanalysis. However, I appreciated Quinodoz's comment that all candidates should be trained to recognize, understand and deal with primitive/psychotic organizations as well as neurotic organizations. Since many patients presenting for treatment now, including training patients on psychotherapy courses, have severe personality disorders, trainers and supervisors need to be aware of and prepared for patients with primitive/psychotic areas and perhaps, another frequent comment in the emails, require a diagnosis from the assessors or referrers.

Therapeutic change comes about through modifying the patient's internal objects or object relations, although the extent to which different therapists rely on the transference in their work varies. Some analysts more actively pursue the transference, constantly presenting themselves as transference figures, real or wished for, reworking and working through, while others are more shadowy, letting the patient get on with it, hanging back until, like the blacksmith, s(he) can strike ‘when the iron is hot’, and some believe that extra-transference interpretations make up a large part of the work. Balint was a psychoanalyst who believed that too much interpreting in the transference meant encouraging a regressive clinging to the analyst, something that he termed ocnophilia. In Balint's terminology, the ocnophile is distinct from the philobat who loves empty spaces and avoids objects, regarding them as a nuisance or a threat. Jackie Gerrard, using one of Balint's clinical vignettes and three of her own, argues that clinging is a symptom of failure in the patient's development that needs sensitive analysis in the transference in order to understand and to dispel the tendency to cling.

Jeremy Holmes

Jeremy Holmes

Raleigh Park, Barnstaple, Devon, EX31 4JB. [Email: j.a.holmes@btinternet.com]

Jeremy Holmes  

The paper considers whether the ideal of a ‘national psychotherapy service’ is a realistic or desirable possibility. In its origins community psychiatry was inextricably linked with psychoanalysis and group psychotherapy. Today the links between community psychiatry and psychotherapy are much more tenuous, despite the evidence for the effectiveness of many psychological interventions in psychiatric disorders. Future psychotherapies will explore the links between brain and mind, integrate the different psychotherapeutic modalities, consider the wider costs of not providing psychotherapy, and be more client responsive. How will this come about? Authority in the field depends partly on seniority, partly on evidence, partly on popular appeal, and partly on psychotherapeutic narratives which accurately reflect the needs of society and those who suffer from psychological distress.

This text discusses theoretical dilemmas posed by the treatment of pre-verbal patients who present themselves as ‘out of reach’, like autistic and mentally delayed children. Darwin's Worms by Adam Phillips. Published by Faber and Faber, London, 1999; 139 pages; £7.99 paperback

James Taylor

James Taylor

London

James Taylor  

In recent times, Adam Phillips has had the dubious privilege of being called ‘the closest thing we have to a philosopher of happiness’. Pleasant as this envied or enviable label might initially sound, it brings with it the burden of our expectations, which, in a sense, is what Darwin's Worms is all about. After Freud and Darwin, what do we want and what can we expect from the lives we have? Where do we get our ideas about such things and what weight should we give to the conflicting messages we are given? What would make us want to live if our sole relief from the transience of existence is the fact of death? And, with all this in mind, is there too much suffering in the world - or just the right amount? (p. 3). It is with this last concern that Phillips begins what is probably his most accessible book to date, a book written with beguiling ease about ‘the big questions’ we inevitably face later, if not sooner. A book that suggests a life is more affirmed than diminished by the constraints of time and knowledge, that curiosity is best engendered by thwarted ideals and that a refusal to mourn is tantamount to a refusal to live.

To this end Phillips recounts the ways in which Freud's and Darwin's thought erosively shifted our sense of ourselves from the theistic worlds of permanence, transcendence and afterlife to the secular transience of (post) modern life. An era in which ‘the present never catches up with the past’ (p. 8), where ‘the past tells us nothing reliable about the future’ (p. 8), and where suffering is the inevitable consequence of the conflict of instincts and the scarcity of resources. However, he suggests we might be more relieved than (narcissistically) wounded to leave behind the old conceptual muddle that made us at once a part of and apart from ‘nature’. In what for me is the most inspiring part of Darwin's Worms, he describes the ways in which Darwin subtly and radically reconstructed morality to include our adaptability, retrieving our ‘fallen selves’ to leave in what we are and do. For Darwin, (our) nature was both creative and destructive and, while the story of ‘natural selection’ brought with it a myth of progress, the direction in which it progressed became random and unpredictable: bad pews for those essentialist traditions in which the map had been sought ahead of the territory. Which is where the worms come in, effectively, as Darwin's advocates, ‘sugaring the pill’ of his ideas. Perhaps echoing the old Christian hope that ‘the last shall be first’, he bucked the traditional hierarchy of ‘higher’ and ‘lower’ creatures by noticing how, like ‘good humans’ the worms worked diligently and voraciously to survive and reproduce. Like Freud, he suggested that the surface was the end of a process or story and that it was the unwittingly collaborative and altruistic worms who had ploughed the earth's surface, long before the idea of a plough had occurred to man. In consequence, there was a soil replete with nutrients, yet they did these things without meaning to. With great subtlety Darwin replaced a purposive myth of creation with one of ‘secular maintenance’ (p. 58) leading Phillips to suggest, ‘it might be more marvellous when the world happens to work for us, than to believe it was designed to do so’ (p. 59).

Diana Priestley

Diana Priestley

Diana Priestley  

This is a timely book which provides an overview of the historical origins of assessment in psychoanalytic theory and practice, the current state of debate and research, and several contributions from psychotherapists working in the Clinical Services of the British Association of Psychotherapists.

In her foreword Margaret Tonnesmann clarifies some confusion which can result from different approaches to assessment which have reflected a move from the symptomatic diagnostic approach of early psychoanalysis and psychiatry, together with estimation of intelligence, ego strength and motivation, towards the use of the concepts involved in early object relations which determine mental and psychic health. This requires the assessor to attempt some use of transference/ countertransference in the process in order that both parties can discover if ongoing psychotherapy could be helpful. She points out that ‘diagnosis of illness is only important at the borders’. That is where we need to be alert to overt psychosis, suicidal impulses or acute acting out.

In their introduction the editors stress the importance of assessment in a climate of a range of therapies being offered. And the necessity of establishing parameters in which it is made clear what can or cannot be offered by a psychoanalytic psychotherapist in private practice. It is an incredibly hard task. In one meeting between two strangers there is an expectation to differentiate between those for whom the psychoanalytic method is not appropriate and who may benefit from another form of treatment, and those who can make a serious commitment to intensive work.

In view of this undertaking which cannot escape the inherent dangers of deciding what is best for someone, it is perhaps understandable that I found some of the outlines for assessment and technique sounded rather imperative. There are a lot of ‘musts’ and for anyone embarking on this work it would be formidable to encompass a social and developmental history, whilst ‘gaining access to the inner world’, combining a classical approach with some degree of structure, observing countertransference, looking for ‘libidinal development, ego functioning, oedipal status, depressive position, not forgetting psychological mindedness, an acceptance of the unconscious, and an ability to use the transference’. And making sure there is a social support network. And explaining the ‘process required’.

Film Reviews

Andrea Sabbadini

Andrea Sabbadini

Andrea Sabbadini  

This is the first in an occasional series of arts reviews that we plan to publish alongside the regular book reviews. The medium is film in this issue, but we hope eventually to cover all media, applying psychoanalytic thought to the various meanings of an artistic object in itself, or as a representative of an artist's repertoire. Reviews are invited on any art form from music to television soaps to anything that can be considered a created object. Please contact Carol Topolski, Book Reviews Editor, 7 Belmont Road, London SW4 OBZ. Tel. 020-7627 0607.

The Attraction of Fear: Some Psychoanalytic Observations on Alfred Hitchcock's Vertigo

The relationship between psychoanalysis and cinema is complex and fascinating. To begin with, they are both young disciplines, just over a century old; in fact they happen to share the same birthday - the screening of Louis Lumière's first films in Paris coinciding chronologically with the publication of the first psychoanalytic book, Studies on Hysteria, by Breuer and Freud (1895). Alfred Hitchcock was born with Die Traumdeutung four years later.

But there is plenty more that cinema and psychoanalysis have in common. They both allow, indeed encourage through a process of free associations (mostly visual in one case, verbal in the other), the exploration of deep emotional meanings in our existence and of the often uncertain boundaries between reality and fantasy. Gabbard (1997) has suggested that ‘to a large extent, film speaks the language of the unconscious’. Dreams, for example, which have such a central place in psychoanalytic theory and technique, use a similar idiom as do many movies - symbolic expression, condensation, displacement, flashbacks and editorial cuts leading to distortions of time and space.

Alongside semiological studies of the film language and ‘deconstructive’ approaches to cinematic (as well as literary) texts, psychoanalytic theories have been since the 1960s the most influential in academic film criticism, especially on the pages of such prestigious journals as the Cahiers du Cinéma, Screen and Discourse. Some authors have concentrated on the interpretation of the content of a film - its subject, its central themes, the treatment of its characters - as if it corresponded to the ‘material’ brought by patients to their psychoanalytic sessions, noticing, for instance, the defensive mechanisms displayed by the protagonists in their relationships or some specific associative links between past events and present experiences. Hitchcock's Vertigo, as we shall see, lends itself well to this kind of textual analysis. Other authors, more controversially, have focused on the analysis of the sociocultural background, the personal history, the character or even the psychopathology of film-makers as they manifest themselves through their works. In this biographical or pathographical perspective, a film - or indeed any other product of creativity - is studied as if it were the symptom of its auteur's existential or interpersonal problems.
