Lady Skelton (Margaret Lockwood) tires of life and husband, Sir Ralph (Griffith Jones) and becomes, in secret, a cross-dressed highwayman. On the road she meets another outlaw, Captain Jackson (James Mason) with whom she falls in love. When she discovers his infidelity to her, she betrays him to the authorities; and later shoots him. Meanwhile, she falls in love with Kit (Michael Rennie), but he rejects her once she reveals her identity as the highwayman. She dies alone, fatally wounded by Captain Jackson, and her husband is free to marry the woman (Patricia Roc) whom he had forsaken for the Wicked Lady.

The Wicked Lady was one of a number of films made at Gainsborough Studios that in their melodramatic, openly erotic thematics, often embroidered by period or exotic settings, deviated from dominant trends in the British cinema of the 1940s. These films were hugely popular with audiences of the day, and were the products of a regular team of writers, directors, stars and other creative personnel. Fargo - A Contemporary Fable (directed by Joel Coen, writers Joel Coen and Ethan Coen, 1996)

Elizabeth Reddish

Elizabeth Reddish

London

Elizabeth Reddish  

Fargo, North Dakota. A frozen, bleak, boundless terrain. The watery yellow headlamps of a car. The watery lifeless eyes of its driver as he walks into the downmarket ‘King of Clubs’ bar. Meet Gerry Lundergaard - a lost soul. The opening images of Fargo offer us a void abundant with meaning.

It is in the nature of conventional cinema narrative, the three-act structure so familiar to screenwriters and film theorists, that it can be read as the systematic depiction of Good's triumph over Evil, of Eros' domination of Thanatos: in psychoanalytic terminology, a transition from paranoid-schizoid splitting to the toleration of depressive ambivalence. Fargo is no exception: a fine example of a story well told.

However, Fargo is at the same time an exceptional film in the construction of its narrative, in its management of resolution and, most specifically, in the nature of its ‘force for Good’. Fargo leaves us not just with the expected sense of closure or resolution; satisfaction that justice has been done, but something more. As the perpetrator is driven away in the closing moments, the sense of resolution is accompanied by a stabbing poignancy, a sudden realization that this story has been about something far deeper than we suspected or than it purported to be. What is the added dimension at the heart of Fargo? What is it about Detective Marge Gundersson's open, enquiring face that lingers in the mind's eye long after her image has left the screen?

The psychoanalytic concepts and ideas of Wilfred Bion are rooted in his pioneering psychoanalytic work with groups. His work posits compelling evidence to support the view that it is only through our relationships with other people (the ‘container/ contained’ model), that we can possibly come to know our own mind. Inherent to this view is the notion that every one of our gestures and thoughts made in relation to others has its parallel in an internal landscape.

It is Fargo's preoccupation with community and the group which underpins its impact. The brutal violence that is visited upon the particular community of Brainerd one night is all the result of one action by one man, Gerry Lundergaard, who, crucially, never commits any act of physical violence at all.

Wild Strawberries (directed by Ingmar Bergman, 1959; available on Tartan Video)

Marguerite Valentine

Marguerite Valentine

Marguerite Valentine  

In its evocation of the unconscious, the film is like an analytic session. Like an interior dialogue a film conveys an interplay between what was seen, and what was experienced, and invites the interpretative skill of the viewer to make sense of what is shown. The interpretation lies in the space between the narrative and the medium of the film. It is a kind of reverie, and the dark, warm intimacy of the cinema develops a possibility to reconstruct a safe, preverbal environment.

The film-maker has a number of techniques at his disposal to communicate his story. Bergman usually shot in black and white, denoting a past, dreamlike state. Through the contrasts of harsh sunlight, the contours of an abstracted and exterior landscape could be lit up or thrown into shadow. His use of the close-up shots which merge one face on another, the distant shot, and the selective use of the frame provide a careful mise-en-scène for the narrative. The viewer is drawn into Bergman's dialogue, and experiences herself as both subject and object. She becomes an active participant in the creative process.

Wild Strawberries is regarded as one of the greatest of Bergman's films. The title is significant. The wild strawberry flowers and fruits in the short Swedish summer, its presence representing a fleeting beauty and happiness. The film tells of Isak Borg's journey from Stockholm to Lund, to collect an honorary degree marking his 50 years' work as a scientist. It is in fact an account of a psychic journey. The viewer accompanies Isak who, through a series of encounters both real and imaginary, finally comes to recognize his own egotism and indifference to others. One might presume that the film is a profound exposition of Bergman's struggle to resolve and to redeem his relationship with his father. At the time of writing in 1957, he had cut off contact with his father, a Lutheran minister, for two decades.

Bergman describes his childhood as filled with repression, fear and loathing. He was punished by slapping but also a more refined type of punishment was utilized - silence. Bergman writes his parents lived ‘in an exhausting state of crises with neither beginning or end’ (Bergman 1988, p. 134). The roots of Bergman's creativity lie here in his early years. His special contribution is his capacity and ability to transform this cruelty into works of art.

The Identification and Characteristics of the Partially Dissociated States of Patients with Borderline Personality Disorder

Katya Golynkina, Anthony Ryle

A developmental and structural model of borderline personality disorder is described. Partial dissociation provoked by trauma and deprivation in childhood is seen to result in the persistence of separate self states. The characteristics of these and alternations between them are seen to account for the main features of the condition. The identification and characterization of states through clinical procedures and the use of the states grid are described and case illustrations are given. The states identified by the grid method in a series of 20 borderline patients are described and classified into six groups, named abuser rage, victim rage, passive victim, ideal, coping and zombie. The clinical value and nosological implications of the model and these findings are briefly discussed.

Religious and Ethnic Group Influences on Beliefs about Mental Illness: A Qualitative Interview Study

Marco Cinnirella, Kate Miriam Loewenthal

An in-depth qualitative interview study is reported, with respondents (N=52; all female) from the following urban-dwelling religious groups: white Christian, Pakistani Muslim, Indian Hindu, Orthodox Jewish and Afro-Caribbean Christian. Qualitative thematic analysis of openended interview responses revealed that the degree to which religious coping strategies were perceived to be effective in the face of depressive and schizophrenic symptoms, varied across the groups, with prayer being perceived as particularly effective among Afro-Caribbean Christian and Pakistani Muslim groups. Across all non-white groups, and also for the Jewish group, there was fear of being misunderstood by outgroup health professionals and, among Afro-Caribbean Christian and Pakistani Muslim participants, evidence of a community stigma associated with mental illness, leading to a preference for private coping strategies. The results lend further support to recent calls for ethnic-specific mental health service provision and highlight the utility of qualitative methodology for exploring the link between religion and lay beliefs about mental illness.

[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale  

Getting down to the nitty-gritty of the dilemma of the would-be psychotherapy patient is the task of clinical assessment: that is, getting a feel for the internal state of the object relations and the external problems in the person's life situation. Then comes the testing of the person's capacity for withstanding the rigours of the interpretive process, the strength of the personality to own and to bear the disturbing emotions that emerge on the road to insight and change. The first programme of the BBC TV series The Talking Cure presented a rare chance to view this process in Caroline Garland's assessment at the Tavistock Clinic of the suitability of a young man for pychodynamic psychotherapy. In our Special Clinical Commentary we print the responses of three clinicians to the interviews, which bring up the important question of how much can and should be done in the initial assessment sessions.

How does the patient know, how can she/he trust, that the therapist will be able to contain and to alleviate the pain of the failure of previous object relations? Required for this kind of trust are not only the initial leap of faith propelling the patient into therapy, but also actual experiences of relief gained from the beginning and from the ongoing nature of the therapeutic relationship as trust grows. More than relief from pain, the integration, development and growth of the personality are desired and conceptualized in different ways in the psychoanalytic literature. Gabriela Mann's article in this issue discusses Christopher Bollas's concept of the functioning of the therapist as a ‘transformational object’, based on the care given to the infant by the ‘environmental mother’. It is this transformational function of the analyst and the setting that fosters a generative or creative environment of internal associations and ultimately alters the traumatized self. Mann brings in by way of contrast two of Bollas's analytic objects that defensively ‘conserve’ or ‘terminate’ psychic growth, challenging the analyst's transformational power, and she offers clinical examples from her practice that illustrate the influence of Bollas's ideas on her work.

Modes of Therapeutic Relationship in Kleinian Psychotherapy

John Nuttall

John Nuttall

6 Vaughan Avenue, London W6 0XS. [email: johnnuttall@tinyworld.co.uk]

John Nuttall  

‘Klein seems to take us to the limits of what is imaginable about psychic life’ (Stonebridge & Phillips 1998, p. 3) and brought new techniques to child psychoanalysis. She probably brought very little new to the technique of adult psychoanalysis. It was left to her followers to develop a distinctly Kleinian approach to psychotherapy, which today emphasizes the emotional immediacy of the patient-therapist relationship. This paper explores the multi-faceted nature of the therapeutic relationship in contemporary Kleinian practice by using as a template the five modes of psychotherapeutic relationship Clarkson identified from her researches, and published in this journal in 1990. Following a review of Kleinian metapsychology, the five modes are discussed individually to show in what way each is manifested in the Kleinian approach. The conclusion is that Kleinian psychotherapy contains, as part of its ontology, the five modes of therapeutic relationship elaborated by Clarkson, and as a corollary offers a postmodern perspective on psychoanalytic psychotherapy.

Jennifer Johns

Jennifer Johns

88 Nightingale Lane, London SW12 8NR

Jennifer Johns  

This paper was given as the second Annual BCP Lecture in November 1999. It addresses the paradoxical position of psychoanalytical psychotherapy at present, pointing out that Freud's ideas are frequently attacked while at the same time being common currency, and the situation in which our ideas are quoted but our referrals drop. The paper questions the extent to which we ourselves are responsible for this and the ways in which our profession itself has become rigidified, clinging to old patterns of behaviour, especially in relation to training, without understanding either the reasons for the outdated patterns or the need to adapt and change them. It is suggested that unconscious disappointment in our work may contribute. Regretting the fact that in this country we are an ageing profession, solutions from other countries are discussed. Finally it is suggested that we can, if the profession so wishes, make appropriate changes here.

Psychoanalytic Applications: ‘It is Myself That I Remake’: W.B. Yeats's Self Construction in Life and Poetry

Paul Schimmel

Paul Schimmel

PO Box 37, Roseville, NSW 2069, Australia

Paul Schimmel  

W.B. Yeats is one of the pre-eminent poets in English of the twentieth century. His verse is characterized by its accessibility and emotional power, and a meticulous craftsmanship in the service of achieving the desired effect. Yeats paid a similarly workmanlike attention to the task of creating his own identity, in a self-conscious attempt to ‘remake’ himself. This paper examines Yeats's life and poetry in order to explore the psychological origins of both his artistic creativity and his need to remake himself. It looks beyond his identification with his father's literary and artistic ideals, to evidence from the poetry for an early developmental experience of absence or failure of the maternal function. The available biographical detail from Yeats's childhood and family is consistent with this conjecture.

Jennifer Silverstone

Jennifer Silverstone

Jennifer Silverstone  

I grew up and became an adult in a time and in a society that didn't want to listen, or perhaps was incapable of listening… It is so easy to make a child mistrust his own reflections, to take away his voice. I wanted my own certainty back, and I wanted my voice back, so I began to write… As a child I also received a new identity, another name, another date and of place of birth… Legally accredited truth is one thing - the truth of a life another. (Wilkomirski 1996, p. 53)

Binjamin Wilkomirski is writing about his past in the present, and explaining the resistance he encountered in the society in which he grew up. He is asking us, the readers of his book entitled Fragments, to understand that society as a whole, and his foster parents specifically, shared an inability to believe in the unbelievable and to think the unthinkable. Like a modern day revisionist, he was brought up, and surrounded, by those who did not believe that he had survived the Holocaust; whether they believed in the Holocaust as an historical event in its totality is not absolutely clear. This text, because it has been challenged in so many ways, now raises core issues within several current debates.

The central debate from the literary perspective rests on the belief and the author's statement that he has written his book autobiographically; he writes as a witness of historical events and claims that he was there and these events happened to him. The publishers have now withdrawn the book because he has been accused of bearing false witness, of not only being absent from the events he describes, but of falsifying his life, his name and his personal story. Alongside this perjury, he has appropriated an event, a religion and a culture to which he does not belong. This part of the debate on the veracity of the text can be placed in the context of Holocaust writing and Holocaust memory that is itself a complex and fascinating area of study.

However the book has been read by many historians of the Holocaust, survivors of the Holocaust, and also average readers who may themselves have scant knowledge about the nature of the Nazis' final solution. Many readers have been deeply moved by the text, and indeed enlightened by it. It has touched people. So a further question needs to be asked: if this text is a false one, in what way is it a falsehood and in what way does it convey a sense of truth? For those who do not believe it, what is the ‘it’ they don't believe? If it is a truth, what kind of truth is it?

Kate White

Kate White

Kate White  

I have a very personal interest in a book about sisters, being the youngest sibling in my family with an older brother and sister. The topic of siblings has been one I have both reflected on and puzzled over for a number of years, and my interest has grown because of the relative absence of theorizing within the world of psychotherapy about the impact of this relationship. I note that the editor of this anthology also comes to her subject from deeply personal experience, both as a twin sister and having a younger sister and brother. It is this autobiographical thread which, I think, is the book's strength, drawing on personal experience to introduce each chapter.

As a psychotherapist I have been fascinated, concerned and sometimes shocked by the powerful impact of sibling relationships on the life of my clients as together we reproduce, experience and unravel their ghosts in the therapeutic encounter. I would describe individual psychotherapy and specifically psychoanalytically oriented psychotherapy, unlike group analysis and family therapy, as being ‘parentocentric’. The focus on and scrutiny of the parent-child dynamic may miss altogether the impact of a brother or sister in a client's struggle for intimacy and attachment. It is notable that current attachment research seems to be bearing out the significance of an association between a person's security with regard to their primary caregiver and their capacity for collaborative and more harmonious sibling and peer relationships (Volling & Belsky 1992).

I think that the apparent absence of sibling narratives in the arena of individual psychotherapeutic work is possibly a reflection of the relative invisibility of this relationship in Western cultures generally.

Editorial

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale  

The psychotherapy debate has currently taken the guise of ‘romantics’ versus ‘postmodernists’, that is, the former who still believe in a ‘big idea’ that informs an overall world view, the latter ‘eclectic’ group who take up therapeutic ideas as needed or useful for whatever the present context, and who question the existence of objective reality and thus any ultimate truth, placing their trust only in the communication between two subjectivities. Less polarized are the integrationists, the practitioners who, echoing the trend toward newer hybrid disciplines in academia, have taken up the view that enrichment comes from interaction with other fields of knowledge. In this issue, Anthony Bateman reminds us that Freud himself was an integrationist when he recommended a combination of behavioural and analytic techniques for the treatment of agoraphobia. Bateman suggests that integration is quietly taking place at a theoretical and clinical level as cognitive behavioural and analytic practitioners use each other's techniques and theories, bringing integration closer than we think. Jeremy Holmes, too, presents his own integrationist approach in this issue, in which he views psychoanalytic ideas converging with attachment theory, linking in neurobiology, neo-Darwinism, infant research and Kleinian formulations.

Advances in brain research and their application to psychoanalytic understanding move ahead. The work of Mark Solms, Antonio Damasio, Allan Schore and others have led to notions of the way mental processes are located and organized in the brain. The research findings suggest that there are three centres found in the brain that can be identified with body awareness/emotional activity, knowledge of reality and the organization of the self, the latter of which is believed to mediate consciousness. It has been suggested that these three centres map the traditional psychoanalytic concept of the ego. Interesting to imagine applications: measurable changes take place through treatment and discernible psychopathology found when one centre takes precedence over the others. These measurements may not be too far away, as, according to an article in The Guardian (6 July 2000), researchers at University College London found that areas in the brain (the medial insula and three others) are active when subjects are in love, as measured by scans showing blood flow. In this issue, Joseph Schwartz writes of his experience of the lecture series given at the Anna Freud Centre, ‘A Beginner's Guide to the Brain’, presented by neuropsychologist and psychoanalyst Mark Solms on the relationship between the mind and the brain, a field which is just beginning to yield its fruits.

Containing Anxiety at the Crisis Centre

Cath Sunderland

Cath Sunderland

Cath Sunderland  

My background is in psychiatric nursing, and it is through my training as a psychiatric nurse that I came to do a placement at the Arbours Crisis Centre, before becoming a resident therapist. I did not realize how influenced I was by the implicit and sometimes explicit assumptions held by the discourses of psychiatry and nursing, nor how some of these attitudes mirrored my own attitudes and ways of coping. Some of the aims of psychiatric nursing are to make people feel better, eliminate symptoms, control feelings, get rid of or suppress difficult feelings, and maintain a ‘professional’ distance (which involves not becoming involved with nor emotionally impacted by the patients). I wanted to think that these were aims I never believed in, but they proved hard to shake off. They even at times felt more ‘sensible’ than living with disturbance in the way we do at the Crisis Centre. At times I've longed for the security of psychiatric terminology, hospital procedures, and the certainty (however illusory that is) offered by these ways of thinking about and responding to emotional distress. At times the Crisis Centre has felt like a ‘mad’ place from which I've wanted to escape.

The response by mainstream psychiatric services is often to treat the feelings felt by the guest and those around them as abnormal and dangerous, something to be somehow got rid of. The anxiety felt by hospital staff is alleviated by adherence to a variety of procedures, which constitute the very fabric of the hospital structure. At the Crisis Centre we try to hold anxiety for our guests in a different way. We aim to contain it in ways which give the guests the opportunity to begin to find ways of eventually containing it themselves. Guests need to come to the Crisis Centre generally because they need to be ‘inside’ somewhere, or something safe. Hospital can provide asylum/sanctuary in a certain way and to a certain extent. Patients are kept physically safer in hospital through the use of external controls: locked doors, seclusion rooms, chemical and physical restraint. Giving sanctuary, a sense of being in a safely bounded space, is one function of containment and one which, in my experience, is in some way provided by hospitals, but provided differently by the Crisis Centre. The holding at the Crisis Centre is different in that it is, on the whole, not physical, but something more emotional and mental. The ‘nursing’ provided is a nursing with thinking rather than action. A second function of containment is to give meaning to experiences that feel unbearable and unthinkable. It is in the provision of this second function that the Crisis Centre differs most from hospitals.

Andrea Sabbadini

London

Andrea Sabbadini  

Anorexia and bulimia, the eating disorders on the border between psyche and soma which are the subject of Gabriella Ripa di Meana's excellent book Figures of Lightness have acquired in contemporary psychopathology, and in the public's mind, a status not dissimilar to that held a century ago by hysteria, also a condition mostly affecting women: diseases of (post)modernity expressing the subject's alienation from what is conventionally expected from her - a construction of femininity, sexuality and subjective identity she does not recognize as her own.

Anorexia1 refers to deliberate self-starvation - starvation of one's self as well as of one's body - characterized by an enormous emotional investment in food, which is however ingested in amounts barely sufficient to physical survival. Bulimia, on the other hand, involves the gorging of oneself with large amounts of food, only to be expelled after a binge through self-inflicted vomiting or abuse of laxatives. Some authors (e.g. Farrell 1995) emphasize the differences between these two conditions, especially as many bulimics, unlike anorexics, manage to maintain a normal body weight. Others, including Ripa di Meana, are convinced that anorexia and bulimia - which share a narcissistic obsession with physical appearance, or rather with a distorted mental representation of it - are so intimately related to be but different manifestations of one ‘mixed, polymorphous psychopathology’ (p. 153), sometimes referred to by the neologism ‘Bulimarexic’ (Boskind-White & White 1987).

To introduce a discussion on anorexia and bulimia one would be tempted to present first some vital statistics. To say, for instance, that approximately 20% of women in our affluent Western societies suffer at some point in their lives - about 90% of them in adolescence - from a serious eating problem; that around 10% of these patients will die as a result of it; that 88% of anorexics are female, and most of them of middleclass social origin; that some 75% of all women are affected by other sub-clinical eating disorders -an excessive preoccupation with body image, weight, calories and diets severely limiting their existence; that eating problems have increased by 50% in the last 20 years; that, in order to be classified as anorexics, patients have to be at least 15% below their normal weight. And so on.

The contributors to Jungian Thought in the Modern World set themselves the task of describing the development of Jungian thought as applied to the ‘big subjects’. These are the nature and workings of the psyche; the structure and dynamics of the conscious and unconscious; how the personality develops and expresses itself; the emergence of meaning; the significance of culture, religion, and spirituality; the mind/body split; the problem of evil and the existence of God. Francesca Raphael  

‘Spilt Milk’ deals with two dreadful aspects of human experience; the death of a baby at the time of its birth and the psychological breakdown of the postpartum mother. The book is utterly compelling, indeed I read it almost at one sitting, but the material is hard to be with; it took me months to sit down and write about it. Despite the bleakness of the material, the six contributors are surefooted, treading a line that is neither overly sentimental nor coldly clinical, but respectful, thoughtful and humane.

The book consists of six lectures given at the Institute of Psychoanalysis in London during the eighties and nineties, on the subject of perinatal loss and breakdown. It is perhaps inevitable that with several different writers the book has a somewhat uneven texture to it, but this is a small criticism, easily outweighed by the quality of the individual lectures.

There is a generous introduction by Joan Raphael-Leff in which she begins by reminding us that pregnancy, whilst a natural experience, is also one which arouses primitive feelings and can revive archaic feelings from one's own infancy and birth, even when all goes well. When the worst happens and the parents find themselves facing a loss where a baby should have been, the result can be breakdown. Raphael-Leff introduces the reader to the complex and varied technical issues facing the practitioner who finds herself working with not only the new and depressed mother, but with the baby in the consulting room as well. There are plenty of vivid clinical examples that bring the theory to life.

Each of the six lectures focuses on the psychological impact of either losing a baby or losing one's mind at the time of giving birth. The lectures span a wide continuum. Dana Birkstead Breen takes a developmental approach to pregnancy, in which she stresses that in the most ordinary and healthy pregnancy there is a need for substantial introspective work to process the various losses involved in child-bearing. At the other end of the continuum Richard Lucas explores psychotic responses to child bearing, and suggests that postpuerperal disturbance is far more widespread than is generally recognized and frequently goes undiagnosed in the community.

This is a book about the relationship between psychoanalysis and twentieth-century thought. Psychoanalysis is seen here as part of the modernist revolt against positivism at the end of the nineteenth century with Freud still embattled 100 years later as an overarching cultural icon at odds with the particularism and relativism of postmodernity. What is the cultural situation of psychoanalysis at the end of the twentieth century? How should psychoanalysis change to meet the postmodernist challenge?

These are the interesting questions posed by this eclectic set of essays and commentaries. Unfortunately no clear distinction is made between postmodernism and postmodernity and there is a curious lacuna in the area of the seminal thinkers in this territory; no mention of Foucault, Lyotard, Baudrillard, Rorty et al. Foucault, for example, believed that psychoanalysis straddled the main problematic of modern culture - the issue of what is meant by human subjectivity - and Freud was repeatedly given the role of the ‘other’ in Foucault's cultural critique.

Nevertheless, the book is often thought-provoking and stimulating in its juxtaposition of different perspectives. In his chapter on Freud and culture, Carl Schorske gives an acute analysis of the gendered cultural geography of Freud's mind, where, for example, England stood for masculinity, heterosexuality and discipline, while France represented femininity, bisexuality and aesthetic expressiveness.

Don Feasey  

Dear Editor

I enclose a copy of a letter that I sent to the director of the Tavistock Institute shortly after the broadcast of the television programme The Talking Cure. I am saddened by that fact that I never received an acknowledgement of this letter, nor any response at all from the team shown in the programme.

From my standpoint I cannot believe that I was the only person, the only therapist, to be shocked and offended by this display of apparent unconcern for the ethics of confidentiality in psychotherapy. In my opinion I believe that most psychotherapists do their level best to protect the client, not only from breaches of confidentiality but also from impulses to make inappropriate disclosure.

In my view one of the most inane and revealing moments in the film occurred when the psychotherapy team discussed the client's wish to appear on television as a kind of desire for exposure, without attributing the same motives to their own behaviour.

I am mindful of your wide circulation and it is with this thought in mind that I send you this letter for publication, so that it might not be thought that the television programme was of no concern to psychotherapists who try to maintain a concern for good practice, in a world which sometimes appears to treat our concern without proper regard.

It is a sad commentary on our times that I can recall that some 20 years ago, when I was involved in television programme-making, if such a programme was planned, the producers would have employed many techniques to protect the patient from exposure to the public at large. It is not that difficult to do but, of course, it does not make for such ‘compelling television’. It could be argued that the participants, by their very presence in the programme, have given consent to their performance. Logically this must be true. However it is a naive position to hold. This kind of consent is not an ‘informed consent’. The participants have no control at all over what will be shown in the programme. That discretion lies in the editing suite and I believe that no television company will allow participants a final say as to what is chosen to be transmitted to the viewers.

Susie Orbach  

On 5 October, as reporters were giving accounts of the devastation caused by the collision of two trains just outside Paddington station, a cultural shift that had been building since the Dunblane disaster was fully enunciated. Woven into every report by newscasters that day and during the succeeding new bulletins as the extent of the tragedy was being discovered was the statement that ‘survivors of the crash and relatives of the victims are being offered counselling’.

Trying to absorb the horror and shock of the crash along with everyone else, there was something reassuring and comforting to know that this event was being understood not just as a social tragedy or as a political indictment (as indeed it was) but as psychologically significant to the individuals as well as to the country, and that the awareness of this as personal and social trauma would surround the interventions made with people who were directly affected by the accident.

There were two new things about the Paddington rail crash that struck me as novel. The first was the fact of the counselling and the reporting of the counselling, the second was the quite widespread accounts of the outrage people felt. Emotions have always been allowed at moments of great public mourning such as Aberfan, a mining town tragedy in my childhood, Dunblane, or at King's Cross, a fire that similarly shocked a nation. The King's Cross fire was a catastrophe with similarities to Paddington - at least in the public imagination: under-investment, neglect, a demoralized work force doing slip-shod work leading to copious unnecessary deaths. But what was different and new about Paddington was the amount of reporting on the reactions of people - those involved in the crash and those not personally affected but passionately caught up by it, as we all were - in the emotional terms in which it was expressed. We heard rage, we heard anguish, we heard terror, we heard deep upset. We didn't just hear that this was a terrible tragedy, we were introduced to a texture and width of the emotional response that was unprecedented in British public life outside of war. Yes, we had abundant emotions and complex ones expressed around the death of the Princess of Wales, but iconic figures are allowed, indeed expected, to evoke powerful emotions. What stands out about Paddington was that powerful emotions were not hooked to an individual, and thus, if you like, to some extent an expression of projection - our fantasy of who this person is, what they represent for us and so on - but were linked to a public event. Politics and feelings were seen to co-exist.

Words such as deterministic, positivist, scientific have been used to describe Freud's approach to his work. Nineteenth-century science was in search of ‘objective truth’. It took physicists like Planck, Einstein, Heisenberg and Bohr to challenge this view. In this wonderfully allusive, beautifully written book by Bollas, it is Freud's method, the method of free association, that has captivated him. But, in contrast to earlier views of Freud's work, this method, according to Bollas, undermines the entire structure of Western epistemology.

By asking the patient to free associate, Bollas says that Freud ‘released us all to be continuously mysterious to ourselves and to others’ (p. 1). Why mystery, what does Bollas mean? He sees the method as breaking open certainties, not only the pathological certainties of patients, but psychoanalytic certainties as well. There are other aspects to mystery, mental illness, why this dilemma and not that. And, more than that, the psychoanalytic exploration itself is full of mystery. Julian Lousada

Julian Lousada

120 Belsize Lane, London NW3 5BA

Julian Lousada  

I want, given the title of the conference, to start with the good news and that is that I feel certain that there is a future and an appetite for psychoanalytic psychotherapy and its applications. I have little doubt there will always be a cohort of clinicians, patients and academics who are drawn to psychoanalytically informed practice, treatment and scholarship. Furthermore there is, I think, an appetite for psychoanalytic ideas in the many settings that seek to engage (as opposed to avoid) the real difficulty presented by mental disturbance. This appetite, in my view, is predicated on the value that we place on thinking in a context where action, ‘competency’ and outcome are used as a defence against thinking.

So that is the good news. However, it is also true that psychoanalytic psychotherapy appears to be swimming against the tide, and it seems to me we should not underestimate the difficulties that we, as a community, face. My concern in this paper is principally with psychotherapy within the public sector and, more especially, the changed relationship between the private and the public sectors.

In my mind the question is not so much whether psychotherapy has a future. The issue is what kind of psychotherapy, informed by what kind of ideas, and located in what kind of space.

Now for the not quite such good news: it seems to me that we are in an extraordinarily different environment to the one we thought we knew. I am thinking here about the impact of globalization, technology, the impact of the lottery, the transformation of welfare, and the arrival of what Anthony Giddens, director of the LSE, describes as ‘Third Way’ politics. I, as someone who has always been interested in politics, freely admit to not knowing quite how to think in the context of the dilemma that the American sociologist Harvard Daniel famously described, namely that: ‘The nation state [has] become too small to solve the big problems, but also too big to solve the small problems’.

We face a paradox in that, on the one hand, there are ever larger numbers of psychotherapists within and outside the core professions wanting recognition, professional registration, and jobs, to say nothing of a place at the high table of mental health policy, and, on the other hand, a drift in policy in quite another direction, a direction which is informed by outcome, ‘clinical governance’ and the market place, none of which have space for subjectivity. Turning the patient into a customer and service into a commodity is probably the single greatest threat to psychotherapy in the present time.

Prophecy Coles

Prophecy Coles

Prophecy Coles  

Apollo, the patron god of the Pythagorians, vowed that Cassandra's prophecies were never to be believed, after she had rejected him. Science, the patron god of the nineteenth century, gave psychoanalysis the gift of prophecy. Psychoanalysis has rejected its patron god and has not been believed. What fate would have awaited Cassandra's daughter? With this thought-provoking idea, Schwartz embarks upon a history of psychoanalysis in Europe and America. The book is structured around three sections. The development of Freud's thinking in his early years in Vienna and his conflicts with Adler and Jung. A middle section in which he traces the history of psychoanalysis in the US and the contributions of William Alanson White and Harry Stack Sullivan. In the last section he follows the development of attachment theory from its Kleinian origins, the growth of feminism and the contributions of Kohut and Lacan.

Schwartz begins by suggesting that psychoanalysis has been the single most important intellectual development in the twentieth century. It shares with nineteenthcentury science the idea that human perception is the gateway to further understanding, though psychoanalysis claims that it is through free association that the human mind can best be understood. Schwartz, who was a scientist before he became a psychotherapist, argues, with great confidence and authority, that psychoanalysis is not unscientific. He cites the case of biology. Biology was not considered a successful science because it lacked precise mathematical rigour. The discovery of DNA over the last 50 years has demonstrated that molecular biology's success has been as the result of describing specific structures. The fact that molecular biology is descriptive can be accounted for by the fact that it is subject to evolutionary change, whereas the fundamental constituents of matter that make up the subject matter of physics and chemistry are not and are therefore subject to causal laws. This argument allows him to conclude that psychoanalysis, as the study of consciousness, memory and emotions, is more like molecular biology. It is descriptive and needs to be understood in its own terms, that is to say, it is constrained by the search for the best description of human subjectivity. Put like this, psychoanalysis can be said to be a science, but not a science based upon an outmoded nineteenth -century model of science. I have dwelt at some length with Schwartz's argument from biology to psychoanalysis for he marshalls a compelling argument to rescue psychoanalysis from the charge of being unscientific. And this position then allows him lo paint a generous picture, in later chapters, of the conflicts that have been endemic within the theory of psychoanalysis.

The populist and somewhat sensational cover of this book belies the seriousness of its intent. The questions the author asks in his prologue concern the relationship between sex, death and power, the rules society or societies develop to ensure the division of power and desire and, finally, symbol formation and the resulting forms of expression: a high brief indeed. His referential spectrum is no less ambitious and touches on anthropology, philosophy, structuralism and modern culture including children's literature, pop and the cinema.

This makes the book an exciting and thought-provoking read but it is also a short book and therefore does not have space enough to answer all the questions it poses or satisfactorily develop the arguments it evokes. Thus it remains, some of the time at least, journalistic and superficial. This is matched by the style which at its best is witty and debunking, but at its worst irritatingly facile, with direct questions to the reader taking the place of articulated links between chapters. This very criticism is, however, unfair for, I believe, the aim of the book is to look at the problems of our society, a society in transition, confused and rudderless, from a Freudian/Lacanian point of view and to make this understanding accessible to a wide audience. In this he has, in my view, succeeded and some of the chapters are illuminating.

The book is divided into three essays: ‘The Impossible Couple’, in which the author looks at the vicissitudes of men/women relationships, ‘Fathers in Flight’ with its self-explanatory title, and, finally, ‘The Drive’ where the underlying theme of the book, the tension between drive and desire, is explored more fully.

The question of how best to help persons vulnerable to psychoses remains one of society's most important and difficult tasks. The difficulty resides in both the complex and differing nature of each individual and their psychosis, their family and social/

258

group context and also the complex nature of aspects of our society including problematic aspects of current mental health services. The fact that the prognosis for persons with psychosis has consistently been shown to be better in traditional cultures than in the industrialized West is a cause for sober reflection on group processes in contemporary Western society.

Therefore this substantive international multi-author book which takes a panoramic view on psychosis from broad group perspectives is particularly welcome. The editors have performed their task excellently, starting with their introduction that will be of use to both the novice and the experienced clinician. In this Schermer and Pines bring together a wealth of contextual material that outlines the contemporary picture: diagnostic features, biological and pharmacological developments and limitations, theoretical views on the nature of psychosis and its aetiology, research evidence for effectiveness of group therapies and, most importantly, the likely experiences (and disease) for the ‘therapist’ of being involved in a group of persons with psychotic tendencies. This latter point is one that is so rarely given the importance that it deserves and surely underpins any attempt to explain why even those psychological therapies for psychosis for which there is a strong conventional evidence base are rarely implemented.

Many of the chapters in this book are indeed open and honest accounts of the possibilities and difficulties encountered in offering a group approach in different institutional contexts. For British readers, Geoff Pullen's account of the vicissitudes of the therapeutic community movement for psychotic patients in various UK mental hospitals makes fascinating reading. What was particularly sobering was to see so well contrasted the elements that lead to pathological institutionalization, on the one hand, and the serious disturbing consequences of some aspects of the anti-psychiatrists, on the other. It was therefore uplifting to read of the maturity of the Eric Burden Community in Oxford that has for nearly 20 years focused so successfully on the ‘poor prognosis’ schizophrenic.

James Fisher

James Fisher

London

James Fisher  

It is a pleasure to be asked to review a book that can be recommended enthusiastically. Although most of the papers in this collection by the American psychoanalyst, Robert Caper, are already available in journal form, the publication of this book is an important event in that the papers together constitute a major contribution to the clarification of contemporary post-Kleinian psychoanalytic theory. Even though one may have read individual chapters in their original journal form, the clarity of Caper's writing makes a cumulative impact read ‘in the round’, so to speak. Six of the chapters were published in the International Journal of Psycho-Analysis and one in the Psychoanalytical Quarterly, all between 1994 and 1998. Two chapters were papers given at symposia in Brazil in 1996 and 1997 on the work of Bion. To these Caper has added two new chapters which elaborate ideas already discussed in the other papers, tightening the focus of the book rather than drawing the reader into new areas.

In his introduction, the author says that, originally, he had not intended these papers, consciously anyway, to have a common theme, although in retrospect they all seem to explore aspects of the developmental struggle to distinguish self from object. It is one of the strengths of this book that it is not one of those collections of previously published papers that the author then struggles, often in transparently artificial ways, to link together. It is much more as if Robert Caper had decided to serialize his book, much as nineteenthcentury novelists used to do, allowing the reader to follow its evolution. One result is that there is a tone of confidence in the theoretical coherence of Caper's elaboration of Kleinian ideas. And it is remarkable that there is no hint of the polemics which have characterized discussions of Kleinian theory by previous generations of North American psychoanalysts.

I wonder whether this book can be seen as another marker of the move beyond the querulous atmosphere surrounding the discussion of the writings of Melanie Klein which, whatever one's theoretical orientation, is not conducive to thinking. Of course it may simply be true that Caper represents that little pocket of psychoanalysts in southern California influenced by Bion, and that his writing cannot be taken as indicative of a change of mood in American psychoanalysis. Whatever the case this book is a solid contribution to the increasing theoretical coherence of contemporary psychoanalysis and seems a world away from ‘party-political’ tone which has impeded theoretical debate. Caper himself is keen to contribute to the scientific development of psychoanalysis and, if ‘scientific’ is taken to mean something like systematic and open-minded investigation of what we can be said to know, I think he succeeds admirably in this tightly interconnecting set of essays.

Biddy Arnott

Biddy Arnott

London W1

Biddy Arnott  

The conclusions I have drawn from this paper are that Brian has a fragile ego structure in which primitive archetypal defences have not been mediated in his early relationships. His defences control terrifying outbursts of rage, feared abandonment and annihilation. These defences have left him dependent upon others and have restricted his life. I understand he has two main defence structures - a sadomasochistic split and a narcissistic structure. In Jungian terminology, he is caught in the grip of the negative mother complex, which impedes his development and leaves him a puer-aeternus.

Brian has not been able to free himself from his internalized parents whose marriage consists of mother who is a dominant, strong force, unable to tolerate aggressive and sexual messes. And father who is too passive to be able to help Brian untie the incestuous knot. Brian defends against a wish for and a terror of fusion with the mother. The male and female aspects of the psyche are held in a sado-masochistic pattern of relating. There is no interaction in either the internal or the external world that could lead to change. He is stuck in a dependent relationship with mother. He is either identified with her in fantasy, functioning as a sadistic aggressor alongside the terror of the cruel force of his penetrating aggression and the feared damage his ejaculation will cause. Or he splits off from his aggression and he can only make a mess that will result in abandonment, thus becoming his mother's impotent, masochistic son who longs for her reassuring holding (snake and teddy bear).

From fear of Intimacy to Perversion: A Clinical Analysis of the Film Sex, Lies and Videotape

Mary Morgan and Judith Freedman

Judith Freedman

TMSI, 120 Belsize Lane, London NW3 5BA

Judith Freedman  

In this paper we explore themes that emerge in psychoanalytic work with couples, particularly in those couples presenting with sexual problems, from the more ‘ordinary’ difficulties of anxiety about being intimate to the more pathological manifestations in perversion. We examine how unresolved conflict in the internal world, especially in relation to the internal couple, can lead to difficulties in the capacity for intimate relating. We suggest that intrusive projective identification and the use of ‘defensive sameness’ and ‘defensive difference’ serve as defences against intimacy. These defences function to obliterate the reality of the other and it is in this sense that we use the term perversion. Finally, we comment on the difficulties for the therapist who may feel drawn into a perverse arena when working with couples with sexual problems.

To illustrate these themes, we offer an interpretation of the film sex, lies and videotape (Soderbergh 1989). In this film we can observe a set of characters demonstrating the range of these difficulties, with the advantage that we do not encounter any problems about confidentiality.

sex, lies and videotape presents us with four main characters, all of whom have a relationship with each other. The film witnesses the different kinds of couples they form, ranging from the marriage between John and Ann to the more transient liaison between Graham and Cynthia. John is an upwardly mobile lawyer who has just become a partner in his firm. He is married to Ann, and they have a beautiful home in a comfortable middle-class American suburb. As the film opens, we see that he is engaged in a torrid affair with Cynthia, his wife's sister.

Ann is beautiful. She gave up work upon marrying and now occupies herself with looking after her husband and their home. She is obsessive about housework and sees a therapist with whom she talks about guilt and anxiety that the world will be overrun with garbage. She has lost interest in sex but realizes in discussion with her therapist that John seemed to lose interest in her before she lost interest in him. These characters could be a couple coming for psychotherapy.

Elizabeth Wright

Elizabeth Wright

Elizabeth Wright  

The cover says it all: a Ghanaian woodcarving of a woman as bearer of a large phallus/ throne, with two erect child/guards at either side. The title of the sculpture is ‘Female Power’. The phallic mother, the riddle of sexuality for both sexes, is the fantasy that psychoanalysis seeks to reduce. The analytic reading is that she is an infantile identification on the part of both boy- and girl-children with the mother's omnipotence, the mother who has everything.

The book is a collection of the work of three generations of women analysts working within the British Psycho-Analytical Society with women patients. It is divided into three parts, the first dealing with the very early tie to the mother, the second with how such experiences are activated in the process of bearing children, and the third answers the vexed question of the relation of sex to gender, under the title of ‘Female experience in the psychoanalytic process’, the true focus of the book. Each section carries its own introduction. There is also a prologue which deals with the British Society and its debates, the psychotherapeutic relationship and, finally, what the book really seems to be about, gender and the analytic process.

The book suggests that when women analyse women the encounter is privileged by the biological sameness of same-sex bodies which may allow ‘an identification with a primitive maternal imago to explode more vividly in the transference’ (p. 24). In Women Analyze Women (Baruch & Serrano 1988), cited in this volume, the specificity of the female-to-female encounter is raised without making such a claim, arguing rather that in the long run the analyst's sex ‘probably does not make a difference in the transference’ (Joyce McDougall, in Baruch & Serrano 1988, p. 65). In She Speaks/ He Listens (Baruch & Serrano 1996), a later companion volume, the authors interrogate French male analysts about their experience with women patients and provide a general and typically French formulation of the analytic scene, ‘where the speaking subject attempts to reorganize her libidinal structure’ (p. 5). This is a reminder that psychoanalysis is not exclusively dealing with the maternal, that not everything turns on women and children, as much of the book under review implies. There is also the question of desire, in which the encounter with the parents' fantasies is paramount -the Oedipus that already lies in wait for the child: ‘The mother has already a complete programme of fantasies, and the father too; there is a relationship between the three players in the drama… even before the baby was born’ (Green cited in Kohon 1999, p. 47). For Green, as for Lacan, the pre-oedipal does not exist, rather the oedipal pre-exists, earlier even than the discoveries of Klein have it. In any case, despite their differences, both Klein and Lacan have shown that it is fantasy which organizes reality rather than being opposed to it. Choosing a man or a woman as analyst is of great significance for the patient, but this significance will be part of the analysis. What being a man or a woman means is dependent on a discourse, that of the patient, and the analyst has no business to import his or her own fantasies into that discourse. The significance of the gender of the analyst is entirely dependent on the patient's pathology.

John Heaton

John Heaton

London

John Heaton  

Jonathan Lear is a distinguished professor of philosophy at the University of Chicago and also a practising psychoanalyst. He has written two books on Aristotle and important essays on Wittgenstein and he uses the work of these two philosophers to give an interpretation of salient themes in Freud, keeping close to his texts. His work is therefore hermeneutic rather than natural scientific and is a working through of Freud's texts showing how psychoanalysis can unfold from its own conflicts. Rather than trying to preserve an assumed literal truth and just repeating it, which is to keep it under omnipotent control, Lear shows how we must destroy the object. It is in the refinding that it can be used creatively. We can only genuinely love that which is outside our omnipotent control.

Lear argues that Freud's great discovery is not of the unconscious but of an archaic level of mental functioning. Archaic thinking is an early stage of a developmental process on the way towards expression in terms of concepts and judgements. Archaic thought is not thought in the ordinary sense. The point of archaic thought is not to express a wish's demand but to satisfy it.

Clinical Material: The X Family

The reason for the referral by the general practitioner of the X family were that father had sought help for the ‘highly disturbed psychodynamics’ within his family - most notably the difficult relationship which existed between his 17-year-old son, Martin, and the mother. The family had had minimal previous Health Service contact. The X family consisted of father, an academic, who was probably in his early 50s from a middle-class English family, and mother of a similar age from a middle-class Argentinian family. There were two sons, Martin aged 17 and Miguel aged 14.

Our first encounter was with the whole family and a precis of this first session is given for it seems to encapsulate some of the themes that we were to experience more directly in the course of the work with the family.

Father started almost immediately we were seated in the therapy room, prior to any introductions having been made, telling us about Martin's behavioural problems which seem to have gone on over the years and were causing a lot of unhappiness in the family, but mostly between Martin and mother. He added, ‘this might be only my view, everyone will have different perceptions’, and then went on to say how he and his wife had different views as to how to address the problem of Martin and that this was a specific point of conflict between them. The problem seemed to have been one for ever and was something that had never been sorted out. The young man whom we take to be Martin was nodding at his father's account although still no introductions had been made. Mother then seemed to spill out, and spoke passionately about her husband never backing her up and that she could not stand this sort of thing, i.e. bad behaviour, particularly when it was displayed on the streets. She told us that she would fight to stop this sort of thing. Eventually one of the therapists managed to say that it was not clear who was who, the other noting the foreverness of feeling expressed in connection with the problem.

Obsessional Thinking - A Defence against Loss

Sara Cooper

Sara Cooper

Meridian House, 32-36 The Common, Hatfield, Herts AL10 ONZ. [e-mail: sara@rafic.waitrose.com]

Sara Cooper  

In this paper I describe my theoretical thinking and clinical work with a patient suffering from obsessional thought disorder and differentiate this from obsessive compulsive disorder, by its absence of ritualized behaviour patterns. I base much of my thinking on Freud, but suggest that the constellation on which this pathology is based consists of a physically and/or emotionally absent father coupled with inadequate mothering. This precludes identification with and emulation of father as the bearer of the ego ideal so that patient attempts to regress to narcissistic blissful union with an idealized mother. If the primary loss, separation from mother, cannot be negotiated successfully then any loss is felt to be intolerable. Thus obsessional thinking is developed as a defence against loss, an attempt within the psyche to create a situation where nothing is given up, symbolized by the alternating opposing thoughts which never get resolved.

Response

R.D. Hinshelwood

R.D. Hinshelwood

R.D. Hinshelwood  

I must say how pleased I am to be here to celebrate with you - you, Joe, and you, the staff over the years, staff and ex-staff of the Crisis Centre - all your achievements. And to celebrate the reputation you've built up over that course of time. It is also, of course, an honour to be invited to respond to these interesting, elegant papers. In the short space of time each paper was given, they provide a particularly good, transparent window into what the Crisis Centre does.

One of my thoughts about the occasion was that it is a licence for a moment of idealization and self-idealization, which psychotherapists aren't particularly good at. But the occasion isn't for that. I know because Joe wrote me a letter telling me what I was supposed to do. I may as well tell you what he told me to do! His letter says, ‘I think we want you not just to praise us as a unique treatment facility, offering psychosocial interventions for borderline and psychotic people, but to place us professionally in terms of other treatment regimes.’ Well you are, of course, unique, and a moment of self-idealization is not out of place on the 25th anniversary. But I'm going to say a couple of serious things.

Borderline and Psychotic People

You are important for the psychotic people you try to help and treat, but I think there is now a real problem about the borderline side of your work. There are other units around - the Cassel, the Henderson and similar places - who can treat severe personality disorders, the narcissistic, and the borderline cases. And, as many of you may know, the Department of Health have produced money to create two more Hendersons, one in Birmingham and one in Manchester, and to run and research them. This is going to be an enormous increase in the rather small current provision. It is going to have a profound effect on all the other units that are going to be treating borderline patients, and I think the Crisis Centre will have to take account of that particular development.

The services for personality disorders have in some sense cracked the problem, or partially cracked the problem of personality disorders. In a sense you may become the victims of the success in the treatments of personality disorders. And government is now beginning to recognize that. It is the psychotic patients who defeat everybody, and the endless number of units trying to provide humane provision which have been established over the years, and have then disappeared, is quite remarkable. What is more remarkable is your Crisis Centre, which has grown up and has not disappeared. It has stayed here for 25 years, and that's what we're celebrating.

Ten Lectures on the Neurology of Mental Life by Mark Solms at the Anna Freud Centre

Joseph Schwartz

Joseph Schwartz

Joseph Schwartz  

When I was doing a post-doctoral fellowship in mental health research 30 years ago there wasn't much going on that seemed to me to be terribly promising. Work with laboratory animals involved behaviours remote from the human condition while electrodes placed on the human scalp gave signals of such generality that it was not at all clear that anything useful could be learned from them. The only research that seemed at all interesting was the work with aphasic patients. I was quite intrigued by Norman Geschwind's patients among whom were people who could identify colours by matching them but they could not name the colour. Geschwind drew the conclusion that the patient's injury had left colour vision intact but had damaged the links between the auditory and visual cortex, the neural connections between hearing the name and seeing the colour. This kind of research actually seemed capable of unravelling some of the components of human mental functioning, perhaps even with relevance to the aspects of human mental life that seemed so much better elucidated by the methods of psychoanalysis.

By the time I became a clinician I had acquired quite a negative picture of research in the neurosciences. I had found it to be dull and ineffective, overly reductionist in attitude and method, in thrall to the physical sciences and the cult of quantitative measurement and dismissive of the far more interesting subject of psychoanalysis. The appearance of Nobel Prizewinner Francis Crick's elegy to reductionism The Astonishing Hypothesis: The Scientific Search for the Soul (1994) did little to disabuse me of my feeling that by and large neurobiology was in bad hands.

But over the last two or three years, a fine informed critique of Crick's point of view by Mark Solms (1995), some fruitful conversations with Solms himself and two lectures by Allan Schore on the neurobiology of human emotion at the last Bowlby Memorial Conference convinced me that a new grouping of neuroscientists appreciative of psychoanalysis had succeeded in finding out things of interest and possibly of importance.

Treatment Development in Psychodynamic Interpersonal Psychotherapy (Hobson's ‘Conversational Model’) for Chronic Treatment Resistant Schizophrenia: Two Single Case Studies

Sarah Davenport MSC MRCPsych , Robert Hobson MD FRCPsych and Frank Margison MD FRCPsych

Frank Margison

Swinton Grove, Manchester M13 OEU. [email: frmargison@aol.com]

Frank Margison  

trauma; sexual abuse; abusive therapy; perversion

Two cases are presented from a project to develop psychodynamicinterpersonal (PI) therapy (Hobson's ‘Conversational Model’) with long-term severe schizophrenia treated in a locked setting. We present two cases from a treatment development project including a description of the model and its use in this setting with some (anonymized) details of the therapy. The ward milieu can act as a container for disturbed dynamics during psychotherapy, but the lack of progress prior to the psychotherapy suggests that there is also the potential for the ward to reinforce or even replicate the disturbance in the patient's internal world. These complex interactions are considered in the light of the methodology for future studies.

Preliminary outcome data and a description of the positive changes observed are included, but with a note of caution about the difficulty of interpreting outcome findings from single case studies in a complex treatment setting.

Transformational, Conservative and Terminal Objects: The Application of Bollas's Concepts to Practice

Gabriela Mann

Gabriela Mann

PO Box 9220, Kfar Shamaryahu, Israel 46910. [email: post@post.tau.ac.il]

Gabriela Mann  

This paper focuses on Christopher Bollas's contributions to the understanding of transformations in object usage. Bollas has delineated numerous kinds of object usage but has not described the possible transformations that could occur as a result of psychotherapy. The author examines conservative and terminal objects, on the one hand, and transformational objects, on the other hand, as signifiers for the kinds of transformation that are likely to occur in psychotherapy. Two vignettes informed by Bollas's ideas will illustrate how the therapist can facilitate the patient's use of the therapeutic environment that ‘transforms’ rather than ‘conserves’ or ‘terminates’ psychic evolution. The author describes how Bollas draws from diverse theoretical sources, particularly from Freud, Winnicott and Bion. The author also suggests that unrestricted use of different theoretical frameworks is consistent with Bollas's favoring free movement between different modes of interpretation. It is argued that this flexibility of moving between modalities is indeed the chief distinguishing characteristic of Bollas's therapeutic style.

Clinical Commentary XXVII: BBC Programme - The Talking Cure

Joseph Schwartz

Joseph Schwartz

Joseph Schwartz  

In this issue we present a clinical commentary on the first film of the 1999 BBC series The Talking Cure. Based on work at the Tavistock Clinic, the first film presented an account of a four-session assessment conducted by Caroline Garland from the Tavistock Trauma Unit of Jan Gale who, in 1991, had been involved in a motor accident which resulted in the death of the other motorist.

The decision of the Tavistock to allow the BBC to film its work raises questions in the minds of many clinicians about confidentiality and violation of the safety of the consulting room. However, we need to be reminded that the family therapists have been using videotaped sessions for training and for conference presentation for many years.

The filming of Caroline Garland's assessment sessions with Jan Gale gives the psychotherapeutic community a chance to see with its own eyes so to speak what these sessions were like. But, as our commentators emphasize, we must recognize that what we see is no less a construction than any other processed version of a therapy session. The BBC has edited its footage to create what the film-makers feel will be a watchable, lively programme. As such our clinical commentaries are commentaries on what we are shown, not necessarily on what ‘really’ happened in this therapeutic dyad.

Many readers will have had strong professional reactions to the BBC's representation of Garland's sessions, both positive and negative. However, it is vital that psychotherapy begin to move beyond strong reactions to begin to formulate principled criticisms and self-criticisms of our theories and practices. We have asked three experienced clinicians to express their thoughts on these sessions as a way to further constructive engagement between different points of view and orientations.

Although the commentators range in opinion about the effectiveness of the assessment sessions, there is broad agreement on the importance of the major clinical issue that appears in these sessions: the question of how to relate to defences. As a professional community we may all wish to reflect on what our respective theories and clinical experiences tell us about the timing, effectiveness or desirability of challenges to a defence structure. We might further want to reflect on how we might engage productively with colleagues of differing views from our own.

Commentary by an Object Relational Psychotherapist

Susie Orbach

Susie Orbach

London NW3 4HA

Susie Orbach  

Neither psychotherapy nor psychoanalysis are spectator sports. Any attempt to show them televisually suffers from the need to dramatize and narrate what is essentially an untidy process involving at one moment the search for understanding, at another the tolerance for confusion, at another the ability to track the nuance of feeling, the scrutinizing of transference-countertransference dynamics and what, to the untrained

51

eye, would be the almost imperceptible changes in consciousness. Television audiences are not educated to observe such processes: they expect story, drama or explication, and yet, of course, what the analyst and therapist looking at the series are most caught up in is precisely that question of process: ‘how did the therapist conduct herself and what were its effects?’

In this television screening of extracts of four sessions between Jan Gale and Caroline Garland in which the material has been edited and pauses inserted, therapists, patients and the public are exposed to far more of an individual therapist's work than is usually possible. Therapy sessions, despite supervision and clinical seminars, are extremely private matters and, much as one may have experience of colleagues in professional settings, one's inability to eavesdrop on sessions, to see, hear and feel the words, the particular ambience, the physical movements of the participants, the way the words, the pauses, the affects, the bodies play between them and so on limits one's sense of what actually transpires between two people. Thus, it is quite a paradox that a first glimpse at the inside of a session from the Trauma Unit at the Tavistock comes from one made for a million people. Parenthetically, it raises interesting questions about the profession's reticence to film unedited sessions for training purposes.

One strand of Caroline Garland's work with Jan Gale is her focus on thinking and her view that he has been avoiding it. Her specialized neo-Kleinian use of a word, which has a very different meaning in popular vernacular, illustrates the difficulties analysts and therapists have as they try to find a language and a discourse within which to construct their relationship with their patients. Jan Gale tells us that he has spent the last eight or nine years thinking. Garland disagrees. She proposes that he has been avoiding thinking. This theme continues through the four sessions and for the uninitiated and, one assumes for Jan himself, this epistemological clash is disconcerting. What Jan seems to mean by thinking is thinking his way around managing the loss of his father at 12 and the traumatic car accident. He has tried to limit his feelings, to find ways of doing away with them in order to have a viable life. He is describing the operations of his defence structure which have served him reasonably enough for some years, but which have resulted in him feeling empty and losing a sense of aliveness. His attempt to manage himself through the study of Buddhism, an attempt which can be seen as his way of reinforcing this defence structure, has been insufficient and has left him in a psychic limbo land in which the self he wishes to control or rid himself of is still inconveniently around and yet somehow devoid of any generative capacities.

Commentary by a Kleinian Therapist

R.D. Hinshelwood

R.D. Hinshelwood

Colchester, Essex CO4 3SQ

R.D. Hinshelwood  

This 40-minute tape, shown publicly, has a number of purposes: to demonstrate, and argue for, the benefit of psychotherapy; to publicize the Tavistock Clinic, and to announce the work of the Trauma Unit. In addition, no doubt, the programme makers wished to capture audience share. Such a catalogue of aims inevitably leads to conflicts, which are dealt with by various methods.

Since the purpose of this commentary (to illustrate a point of view - Kleinian) is not one of the aims of the programme, a commentary is disadvantaged. Nevertheless, I think that there is enough ‘material’ that inevitably bursts through to take a view.

The programme followed a particular course, one restricted to the content of the patient's communications. It reveals deeper, implicit and unconscious meanings. This is in line with the more cognitive view of interpretation typical of the early days of psychoanalysis. Because it is a more familiar approach the programme-makers, I imagine, relied on it to present ‘the impenetrable ideas of psychoanalysis’ to the uninitiated.

But there are moments when one can get some inkling of a second approach. That follows the process of interaction, the transference/countertransference that is going on between patient and therapist. The latter approach depends heavily on sequences of dialogue between patient and therapist, and, because of editing, these are not often available here.

Psychoanalytic psychotherapy today will attend to both approaches, and picks up where the pattern in one perspective matches the pattern in the other - a binocular view which will point to the eventual interpretation. I shall take these approaches separately and start with the first, the unconscious meanings of the contents of the patient's thoughts.

The Content's Unconscious Meanings

The patient was referred initially by his GP to the Trauma Unit, and the programme records an assessment process of four sessions. Interestingly, the actual trauma - the death of the ‘other driver’ in a road accident - fades out; and the programme diverts to the patient's loss of his father (due to parental divorce) when he was 12, and the personality problems that have arisen from his method of coping with that. The therapist concentrates largely on the latter, the character traits that have become the core of the patient's personality.

Commentary by a Psychoanalytic Psychotherapist

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

Thomas Guy House, 47 Weston Street, London SE1 3RR

Jean Arundale  

On the unusual, even rare, occasion when psychotherapists have the opportunity to view directly another psychotherapist at work, there is an inevitable sense of fascination and privilege. Then, after becoming immersed, one has a more complex response: how to think about the colleague's work when the theoretical orientation or personal style may or, perhaps just as problematic, may not differ from one's own. In the assessment interviews conducted by Caroline Garland at the Tavistock Trauma Clinic, presented on the BBC programme The Talking Cure, we had an invaluable opportunity to witness the working of a highly-trained analytic mind in interaction with a troubled, psychotherapeutically inexperienced young man. Any evaluation of the interviews will require a careful attempt to understand what the clinical exchanges meant, to tease out the psychodynamic theories on which they were based, and to determine whether the assessment was successful in achieving its aims.

The patient is Jan, 30 years old, who sought treatment for a trauma which occurred at age 21 when he was driving a car at excessive speed and hit another car that pulled out onto the road, killing the other driver. Since the crash Jan has experienced little affect related to the accident and a generalized emotional block. Jan trained as an electrical engineer, but at the time of the assessment he was unemployed, living with his Australian partner with whom he intended opening a coffee shop/art gallery. He spent his time painting and listening to music. A significant situation from Jan's background was given from his application form: his parents divorced when he was 12 and afterwards his father left the family. Jan didn't see his father again until he was 20, and then only briefly. Further information given was that he engages in self-destructive behaviour, smokes cannabis, confuses sex with affection and is trying to become a Buddhist.

Clinical Material: Brian

Brian, now 35, has been coming to once-a-week therapy for nearly four years. He lives in a small northern town in a flat he is buying, close to the home of his parents. He comes from what he sees as a typical English family: ‘people’, he says, ‘who never talk to each other about anything meaningful’. He has a brother, four years older than him, whom he greatly admires, a successful, confident man, married with children. Brian said he saw himself as ‘lonely, gawky and gauche’. I noted that I saw him as pleasant, smiling and likeable.

He said he was doing a course for which therapy was essential. It later emerged that it was advised but was not compulsory. He summarized his problems as difficulty in making relationships, lack of confidence, and an inability to confront, and when he really started to talk he said it would be ‘like a watershed’. At this point he was tearful and distressed and showed a depth of emotion that has rarely been repeated.

In the second session Brian said, ‘Things have come to a head.’ He had had a very emotional weekend with his ‘girlfriend’ (here he indicated quotation marks with his fingers). She said she wanted to marry him and have children, but he said, ‘It won't happen’. I queried, ‘You don't want to be with her?’ He reiterated, ‘It won't happen’. The only sexual involvement had been kisses and hugs, but they did nothing for him. I said, ‘What are you telling me?’ Brian replied, ‘I am gay’. The hinted at watershed did not materialize.

Brian was a virgin, had no sexual experience, but was emphatic he was gay; he had known in his teens. In my initial notes I had commented that he ‘seemed virginal, as though aspects of his life were unlived’. He repressed his sexuality because it was so unpleasant, horrid, he didn't want to be like that, he wanted to be normal. He envied his brother's good family life.
